Aromas, colours, flavours – a culinary voyage of the senses out on the panoramic terrace or in a chic bistro-style dining area on the ground floor of the Hôtel de Paris.

Name: Logan Laug
Description: A smart contemporary interior, with white brick walls, green patterned wallpaper, parquet flooring and glazed wine cellars facing the service counter, is the stage masterminded by chef and entrepreneur Logan Laug, who leaves no detail to chance! With his brigade, he crafts modern, fusion cuisine that bears the stamp of his far-flung travels. Examples might include suckling pork chop Tex-Mex style with corn; or red mullet two ways, textures of artichoke and chermoula.

Name: Domus
Description: Domus (Latin for "home") is presided over by a dream team of two chefs and a front-of-house manager who earned their stripes at Michelin-starred restaurants and high-quality bistros (the chefs met at La Table du Connétable in Chantilly). They take full advantage of seasonal ingredients and the produce of the Sologne region to whip up intriguing dishes: mackerel tarte fine with Orléans mustard; skate wing a la plancha, roasted pumpkin and caramelised squash seeds; figs poached in red wine, creamy zephyr.

Name: Frenchie Biarritz
Address: Hôtel Regina Experimental, 52 avenue de l'Impératrice, Biarritz, 64200, France
Description: This restaurant ensconced in a hotel looking down over the bay has been entrusted to Grégory Marchand (of Frenchie). Once past the vast atrium that serves as the bar (where you get a foretaste of all the details of the delightful 1920s-inspired decor), you come to a beautiful dining space and a terrace with sea views. The chef has created a menu inspired by the Basque region and added a few creative touches in a "chic brasserie" style: smoked aubergine, yuzu condiment, grapefruit and black garlic; meagre meunière, artichoke barigoule, tarragon hollandaise, shellfish bisque with vanilla. Extensive wine list (around 15 wines by the glass).

Name: Epicentre
Description: This eatery is located in a side street off the busy Rue Sainte Catherine. From his tiny kitchen at the rear of the dining room, which enables him to chat with customers, chef Benjamin Wavrant whips up a bargain-priced bistronomic lunchtime menu with a patriotic line-up of dishes, like potato soup followed by a slab of pollock seared in butter, flavoured in citrus fruit and underscored by a gutsy meaty gravy. More upmarket in the evening, premium ingredients such as foie gras, scallops and pigeon are crafted into a more gastro-leaning menu.

Name: Le Grand Large
Description: Just a stone's throw from Rémigeasse beach, amidst dunes and unspoilt countryside, Le Grand Large Hotel overlooks the ocean below. The restaurant faces both the indoor swimming pool and the sea, which is perfect for sunset portraits in the evenings. The menu by David Boyer (Meilleur Ouvrier de France) exalts the region’s first-rate produce. The crab with roasted rice and glazed lovage, or the two-course Racan pigeon with a raspberry reduction, bear witness to the chef’s meticulous handiwork.

Name: GAMIN
Description: After a period of hopping from one time zone to another (Alain Passard, Corsica, Dan Barber's Blue Hill restaurant in the US), Bastien and Charlotte Guillochon's decision to set up shop opposite a port seemed entirely natural! Their "culinary house" (as they call it) is open from breakfast to dinner and has plenty of cosy corners. Each dish on the menu starts with the name of a vegetable or fruit: cucumber, shellfish ceviche, camelina oil; round courgette, spring carrot purée, chimichurri, rockfish seabream. This is modern cuisine that is respectful of the environment and devilishly well crafted.

Name: L’Oyat
Description: Even in Paris, near the Place de la République, a Ch'ti chef from Dunkirk like Jérémy Sergeant continues to hark back to the beaches of his native region: marram grass – oyat – is a small plant capable of holding in place the sand of the dunes. In the kitchen, he brings to bear all his experience: the produce is fresh, the style modern and light, the jus tasty and the whole thing smacks of sincerity. In the evening, the menu is subtly embellished with premium ingredients. Cosy, contemporary atmosphere.

Name: Le Noyo
Description: A few minutes’ walk from the covered market, this dinky eatery, refurbished in a tasteful modern vibe, is the brainchild of François Liebaert, a well-known local chef. His enticing seasonal menu is occasionally jazzed up with creative notes, such as line-caught hake served with a gutsy Spanish sauce, flanked by spot-on balanced seasonings and artistic plating. Estelle efficiently and cheerfully manages the front of house.

Name: Au Soleil
Description: Set in the heart of a picturesque Alsace village, this establishment is the epitome of sunny, like its gregarious chef, Anthony Schauer, who trained in top houses in northern Alsace. He and his wife cheerfully welcome you to their tasteful, contemporary restaurant, which provides the perfect foil to fresh, gutsy, seasonal fare with a bistronomic slant, such as marbled parsley ham served with a tangy ravigote sauce or confit of pollock, tomatoes, basil and fennel.

Name: Les Terres Iodées
Address: 64 route de la Corniche, Houlgate, 14510, France
Description: If you, like the Impressionists, are mesmerised by the changing light and colours of Normandy, then you must make a beeline for this restaurant established in a half-timbered inn between Houlgate and Deauville. In addition to parquet floors and light wooden furniture, the spacious, airy dining room enjoys a double exposure. The chef, whose parents ran a restaurant, serves hearty seasonal fare and aims to work with top-quality local produce (Normandy beef, lamb from salt marshes). His loin of pollock with steamed vegetables, smoked stock and an emulsion of sesame is emblematic of his creativity.

Name: Le Moulin de L'Imaginaire
Description: Born and bred in nearby Brive, the chef is an advocate of hearty traditional cuisine, in which local ingredients abound: fried egg, crispy bacon and new-potato galette; calf's head with ravigote sauce; free-range guinea fowl with carrots; moist walnut cake with crème anglaise. This converted mill on the banks of the Vézère (the old cogs can still be seen beneath the glass floor in the entrance hall) has been renovated and transformed into a contemporary bistro. It also boasts a terrace built over the river, facing the 12C Pont Vieux.

Name: Etika
Description: Etika: the name of this restaurant just off the main road on the way to the centre of Bidart sums up the project of chef Alexandre Willaume (previously at Aho Fina). His ethical bistronomy cuisine shows a genuine commitment to carefully sourced local produce, which he places centre stage. His sincere dishes are predominantly fish- and plant-based: tuna belly, anchovy and tomato; clams and citron; apricot and granola. With 80% of the cooking done over charcoal, the dishes are perfectly cooked. At lunchtime, choose from the small tapas-style portions to make up your menu; in the evening, they serve multi-course à la carte menu.

Name: L'Orangerie
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: Comfortably ensconced in the former fine dining restaurant, L'Orangerie is a real treat, indulging diners with an array of options. The most emblematic dishes and recipes of the father of nouvelle cuisine, Michel Guérard, are present and correct. Alternatively, you can get your teeth into fine cuts of meat grilled over an open fire, more ethically reared meats from the Landes area (Blonde d'Aquitaine and Bazadaise beef, local poultry). Then there is the range of starters that combine classical fare and brasserie-style dishes (house-smoked salmon, horseradish cream and toast; avocado "cocktail" and large prawns from Palamós). An establishment that combines nostalgia and an opulent sense of well-being, epitomised by the melt-in-the-mouth raviolo of mousserons and wild mushrooms (served here since 1978) and the dessert trolley.

Name: POPS
Description: Pops is the nest of two fledglings who have flown the snug Mare aux Oiseaux, a recognised talent hatcher helmed by Éric Guérin. In their eatery just off the seafront, Corentin Leverger and Océane Maisonneuve bend over backwards to regale diners with fresh premium, often organic produce such as girolles mushrooms or red mullet. Their creative bistronomic score rolls out a festival of textures and forthright flavours illustrated by a scrumptious tartlet of mushrooms, prepared in several ways (raw, cooked, in jelly, creamed and pickled).

Name: Le Quai
Description: On the banks of the Saône, this quayside brasserie boasts a very pleasant terrace right beside the river. In charge of proceedings is chef Valéry Meulien, who was trained by Jean Ducloux and Paul Bocuse, and later earned a Michelin star himself. His dishes focus on the region's classics, including pâté croûte, ham terrine with parsley, calf's head, and sweetbreads with morel cream. The flavoursome red wine sauce sprinkled with chopped parsley that accompanies the œufs en meurette is proof that the chef has by no means lost his touch.

Name: Notes
Address: Hôtel La Nauve, 12 rue de la Nauve, Cognac, 16100, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: A little way from the town centre, this fine 19C town house is now a luxury hotel. It has undergone first-class restoration work, and this has particularly benefited the restaurant's dining area, which is set in a small lounge. Chef Anthony Carballo proposes two surprise menus comprising several courses, inspired in part by the estate's vegetable garden. Tomato, basil and burrata; pollack, courgette and fish stock: a wonderful gourmet interlude!

Name: Alivetu
Description: This little "olive grove" (alivetu in Corsican) is an oasis for foodies in the Saint Victor neighbourhood, abutting the Colline de la Garde. The restaurant is split into a dining area with a polished concrete floor and a mezzanine, where diners tuck into the chef's Mediterranean cuisine: think grilled octopus, sweet potato purée, corn and pepper sauce. A "Market Menu" on the board at lunchtime and a surprise set menu in the evening.

Name: Sublime
Description: The modern cuisine of Sicilian chef Giovanni Spataro Cammarata encompasses carefully executed French dishes such as turbot, asparagus, aioli and lemongrass emulsion, and emblematic Italian specialities including his take on vitello tonnato. He sources excellent ingredients – turbot, Charolais beef and Sicilian prawns, which he prepares and presents with impeccable taste. The space comprises a pared-back dining area painted white, located just a stone's throw from the covered market.

Name: Épicéa
Description: In a narrow street near the Doubs, this couple, who earned their stripes in prestigious establishments, work in tandem in the open kitchen, occasionally venturing out to serve diners. Their single set menu, based on carefully selected seasonal produce and enhanced by wild-picked ingredients, is akin to a natural history lesson: carrot / marjoram / plantain / burnet / bay leaf; black pork / pumpkin / poultry jus / spring onion oil; beetroot / raspberry / coriander / iced nougat.

Name: Palégrié Chez l'Henri
Address: 66 rue de la Tour, Autrans-Méaudre en Vercors, 38112, France
Description: As enthusiastic as ever, Guillaume Monjuré (who first came to our attention in Lyon and Corrençon-en-Vercors) plays host to guests in this family-owned barn, which has been renovated into a table d'hôte-style restaurant. Fanning the flames of his passion for cooking over an open fire, he has set up a wood-burning oven in full view of diners; he cooks absolutely everything in it, from bread first thing in the morning, to vegetables and fish during the meal. This is natural, primitive cuisine that is no less personal and creative for all that. He is able to elevate vegetables, herbs and fish from the local fish farm, in dishes such as his ikejime char, matured for a fortnight and accompanied by courgettes and herbs from the chef's garden. This free-spirited chef also makes forays into Mediterranean territory, with dishes such as blue crab served with lettuce, horseradish and lovage. The set menus are apt to change daily. Chrystel, who knows her wines like the back of her hand, will be happy to talk you through a fine selection that features plenty of organic and natural options. An authentic and appealing approach to life and to cooking.

Name: Le Bout des Canards
Description: This inn, with its plum and lavender-toned façade, will have a new chapter in its story thanks to its new owners. This couple has worked in some fine establishments (he was sous-chef at Villa René Lalique; she was assistant to the maître d'). In a decor of pale-coloured wood, pick from a short seasonal menu; many dishes are based on local ingredients (eg marinated trout, rocket, horseradish, cucumber and smoked oil, or crispy waffles, caramelised mirabelles and fromage blanc ice cream). The lunch deal is unbeatable value and the welcome is particularly warm!

Name: Thiou
Address: Hôtel Norman, 9 rue Balzac, Paris, 75008, France
Description: Chef Apiradee Thirakomen, who goes by "Thiou", has set up shop on the Right Bank, in a small hotel just off the Champs Élysées. In a chic, intimate atmosphere, you can sample the Thai specialities that have made her reputation. Some have a French twist: prawn ravioli with coconut cream flavoured with lemongrass, pad thai, "Crying Tiger".

Name: L'Alentour
Description: This quintessentially cosmopolitan, downtown eatery of Beaune is the joint brainchild of Tatenda Mhende, in charge of the dining room, who hails from Zimbabwe, chef Natasha Watson, who is from Calgary (Canada) and Marc Marchetti, also a chef, who is a Beaujolais lad. This alchemy of buddies has sparked a particularly appetising culinary offering that is depicted by a concise menu of hearty dishes packed with punchy flavours, to be shared (or not!): barbecued oxheart tomatoes, smoked tomato water and mozzarella; crunchy fritters of mushrooms with marrow, chardonnay-flavoured vinegar gel; pork belly, patty pan squash and courgettes.

Name: Circle
Description: The name of this restaurant pays homage to American rapper Mac Miller, as well as to the circle of friends and co-workers running the show here! Chef Bastian Ruga has perfected his concept. Playing out to a soundtrack of American rap music, his youthful, no-holds-barred cuisine charts a course between bold creativity, North African and Asian influences, and a healthy dose of affection for traditional cuisine – this is Lyon, after all! The original food-and-drink pairings are an integral part of the experience, encompassing beer, herbal teas and a natural wine list. A shining example would be the wonderfully pearlescent cod with black garlic hollandaise sauce, served with a comforting ginger brandade. The style of service is professional and trendy.

Name: Joki
Description: Sweet chestnut soup and mushrooms on toast; duck breast, sweet potatoes and orange sabayon: at lunchtime, this bistro proposes nattily crafted, enticing recipes with a traditional leaning that change weekly. In the evenings, the concept involves food-cocktail pairings and a several course menu, providing the opportunity to showcase premium ingredients like pigeon, oysters, scallops… Located on the ground-floor of a characteristic Bordeaux building in the heart of the historic centre, you can expect a tasteful interior paired with a cosy, relaxed vibe.

Name: Osteria Matto
Description: Chef Thomas Asti has Italian blood running through his veins. So, it made sense when he and his partner opened this bistro-styled trattoria. The duo draws on Italy’s glorious culinary heritage to the delight of their loyal regulars, who flock here to sample vitello tonnato, bagna cauda, veal with house-made potato gnocchi – and Sicilian lemon tart, just the way nonna used to make it. To be washed down with premium Italian wines. What’s not to like?

Name: Lurrak
Description: On the Basque pelota court, there is more to this pretty, traditional Basque building, dating back to the 1900s, than meets the eye, as it now sports a distinctly Scandinavian vibe. This success story is the work of two pals who met in David Toutain's restaurant. Chef Romain Goyeneche's fresh cuisine errs towards sophisticated, with an emphasis on plants and regional produce: green peas and broad beans, rhubarb and trout roe; strawberry, rose honey, fermented milk and fennel. Having spent time in Copenhagen, the chef employs various Scandinavian preservation methods. Paul Chauvet is in charge of the slick front-of-house experience, providing excellent wine tips along the way.

Name: Auberge du Prieuré Normand
Address: 1 place de la République, Gasny, 27620, France
Description: Near Giverny, the main square of Gasny is home to this full-blown Normandy-style, half-timbered family-run inn. The chef favours local produce in his inspired cooking, steeped in gutsy sauces and forthright flavours. His signature dish, risotto of langoustines, is to die for! The interior boasts a bar, a cellar, two contemporary dining rooms and a patio come fine weather.

Name: La Mère Léa
Description: A new start for La Mère Léa, a true local institution, which has expanded on a quayside location and now enjoys more space and a beautiful view of the Fourvière and St-Jean quarters. Lyon specialities still feature prominently, with two good value-for-money set menus and a well-crafted à la carte menu.

Name: Brasserie Chavant
Description: This place in the heart of the city can't fail to make an impression with its chic baroque decor. In summer, grab a table on the terrace overlooking the secondary school (Lycée Champollion) and savour the house's signature dishes: langoustine ravioli, truffles and foie gras; pan-fried squid with Espelette pepper and Basque sauce. "Chavant" was the name of the owner's ancestors, restaurateurs since 1852.

Name: Ma Table en Ville
Description: This is perhaps the archetypal 21C bistro, with its colourful contemporary interior, naked light bulbs and exposed pipes… The chef, who expertly prepares traditional cuisine, is also to be seen in the dining area. He is committed to quality ingredients – a favourite of ours is the cauliflower soup with cashews and poached egg! Good choice of regional wines, and service with a smile.

Name: L'Instant du Sud
Description: A pretty stone house in the heart of a village near the Camargue Nature Reserve is the haunt of an endearing couple. Whether it is on the patio beneath a canopy of reeds or in the small cosy dining room, the vibe is welcoming and professional. The chef wins us over with a concise, contemporary score at eater-friendly prices and a generous hand when it comes to filling the plates. He has a clear fondness for sweet-sour Thai marinades and barbecue sauces. The almond-flavoured pannacotta adds a refreshing light flourish to the end of the meal.

Name: Le 1720 - Château de Sully
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Wheelchair access
Description: Grandiose is the term that springs to mind when describing this 18C château, set in landscaped grounds planted with Lebanese cedars and sequoias. Take a seat in one of the plush dining rooms or in the bright conservatory to savour the chef’s predominantly Normandy-focused cuisine: vegetables, cheeses, foie gras and, of course, line-caught fish.

Name: L'Océan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Great view,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Founded in 1981 by Louis and Yolande André, who are now assisted by their daughter Dominique and son-in-law Gérard Samson, L’Océan is a treat for the eye and the palate thanks to the huge conservatory and a menu that stars supremely fresh first-class seafood and fish. The establishment’s timeless signature dishes never fail to deliver: seafood platters, scallops in season, sole meunière or whole seabass in a salt crust (to be shared). We also recommend the big-boned lobster bisque, rich in whole pieces of perfectly cooked lobster and deliciously crunchy croutons. Finish with a wickedly tempting rum and raisin baba – the epitome of comforting nostalgia as you watch the sun set over the waves.

Name: Maison Burgarella
Description: Between Causses and Aubrac, the Burgarella family ushers you into this tastefully refurbished house. Downstairs, the Table de Romane brasserie celebrates hearty regional fare (calf’s head, tripoux (sheep tripe), while upstairs the swanky gourmet La Tour establishment allows the creative chef, visible from the open kitchen, to give free rein to his inspiration without losing sight of his Aveyron roots. A delicious gourmet halt on the banks of the Lot River under the aegis of Château de Calmont.

Name: Hostellerie La Briqueterie
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This luxurious hotel surrounded by vineyards is still going strong, thanks to features such as plush guestrooms, a rose garden... and its restaurant, in which chef Nawal Rezagui meticulously prepares treasures of the local terroir to create dishes in a bistronomy vein at lunchtime and fine dining cuisine in the evening. The food is beautifully crafted: think cream of white asparagus and crunchy green asparagus with champagne vinegar; veal, artichoke, peas and a veal jus with oregano; cabbage, green cardamom and vanilla ice cream – now to be savoured in a bright, modern dining area, whose large bow window affords a beautiful view onto the gardens outside.

Name: Belle de Mars
Description: Behind wrought-iron railings, this handsome establishment unveils a tasteful interior (white walls, parquet floors, wooden chairs and tables) and an open kitchen helmed by Michel Marini and Kim-Mai Bui. This veteran couple (stints with William Ledeuil, Christophe Moret, Gérald Passedat…) crafts flavoursome, invariably delicate dishes, often sprinkled with herbs they pick themselves. Examples include Camargue oysters, clementines and sabayon and even the appetisers knocked our tastebuds for six with their crisp, expressive flavours. The cheerful, relaxed service is fully in keeping with the vibe of this welcoming establishment. Highly recommended!

Name: L'Atelier Mélanie
Description: This restaurant pays tribute to Mélanie Rouat (1878-1954), a friend of Curnonsky and a two-starred chef in her day. Her great great grandson, chef Jean-Baptiste Caillarec, and his pastry chef partner Laura Martinon, both of whom have previous experience in prestigious establishments, have opened this bright, contemporary restaurant. Soft-boiled egg marbled with port, creamy mushrooms; roast mullet, carrots and sesame; deconstructed apple, caramelised apples, apple and tarragon brunoise, cider emulsion. The duo work meticulously with quality ingredients to create delicious dishes.

Name: Bloom Garden
Address: Bloom House, 23 rue du Château-Landon, Paris, 75010, France
Description: Housed in a brand new hotel, this restaurant channels the spirit of the Mediterranean, with an interior inspired by the South of France. Plants are everywhere, from the wooden floors covered with Berber rugs to the wicker hanging baskets set against a backdrop of zellige-tiled walls. In fine weather, you can bag a table by the pool on the lovely interior patio. Chef Olivier Streiff, who arrived on the scene in 2015 as a contestant on Top Chef, has created a bold, colourful menu that is also inspired by the Mediterranean. Veal tournedos, pan-fried polenta and liquorice; molten chocolate cake with candied pepper; lemon tartlet with chicory chutney: this vivacious chef enjoys gently subverting culinary convention.

Name: Le 6
Description: Le 6 (formerly Le 6 Paul Bert) received a facelift ahead of its reopening with chef Pauline Séné (Top Chef) at the helm. With its bistro-style furniture, zinc-topped bar for guests to eat at, and tightly packed old-school café tables and chairs, the restaurant is in full swing – in fact, it is often fully booked. The appealing menu achieves a balance of delicacy and indulgence, showcasing the ingredient without ever overdoing it, for instance smoked tarama, trout roe, focaccia and wakame; monkfish, celeriac, beurre blanc, blackberry nori and katsuobushi.

Name: Lucas et Chris
Description: Located just a few minutes' walk from the old town, this contemporary bistro with an emphasis on conviviality is run by two guys who were born and bred in Colmar: Lucas Gaertner (in the kitchen) and Chris Roldan, who is also a DJ in his spare time. At lunchtime, the chef serves a three-course set menu (choice of fish or meat); at dinnertime, the menu – updated every month – is more extensive. Expect beautifully prepared dishes that err on the side of tradition, such as salmon gravlax, horseradish cream and honey mustard, or veal kidney and butternut knepfles – a testament to the experience of a chef who has worked at Robuchon and Le Maximilien in Zellenberg.

Name: Symbiose
Description: The name of this restaurant may refer to the close bond between the chef and the sommelière (who are partners in life), or the association of food and wine – the couple’s respective passions, or to the two set menus served in two separate dining spaces. The first is a “tasting bar”, which rolls out dishes to share that tap into influences from far and wide (ceviche of croaker, ceviche juice and guacamole); the second is dedicated to fine dining with two tasting menus (and a third more concise score at lunchtime). The chef, who finds his inspiration in Normandy’s first-class fare and culinary heritage, draws on his years of experience in top flight restaurants to create modern cuisine with just the right touch of creativity. We recommend his new spin on the tarte Tatin with a calvados soufflé.

Name: Terrae
Address: 7 avenue de la Mairie, Cambo-les-Bains, 64250, France
Description: Grégory Ménard and Lucile Voisin (Choko-Ona and Grand Hôtel de Saint-Jean-de Luz) have converted this former fishmongers into a cosily dinky restaurant steeped in stylish appeal. The tasteful interior sports warm terracotta walls, linen-coloured banquette seating, pale wood tables and fine tableware: hand-crafted Basque silverware, cutlery and ceramics. The menu is inspired by the availability of fresh local produce and the chef’s boundless creativity. Pyrenean trout, marbled in squid ink and beetroot pickles; Kintoa pork and Iberic pancetta, medley of artichokes: flavour, colour, hard work and a dash of creativity.

Name: À Table
Description: Camille Guérin has given this former bistro an understated makeover, complete with a light-filled enclosed porch and lovely pale wood furnishings. A concise lunch menu on the blackboard and a single set menu in the evening that kicks off with an assortment of three starters to share. The young chef makes it her culinary mission to put a bistronomy spin on classic French fare, proposing a handful of vegetarian options and prioritising local produce – and she pulls it off with well-crafted dishes at reasonable prices. "Perfect egg" with mushrooms and chopped parsley; roast pumpkin and falafel-style squash galette; beef sirloin with a meat jus infused with sage; textured pear and honey-almond crisp.

Name: Vaisseau
Description: Chef Adrien Cachot has been a familiar face since appearing on French TV's Top Chef in 2020. In a space with a minimalist decor and intimate atmosphere, the chef puts his creativity to the test, creating dishes that often feature unexpected pairings, such as the show-stopping "Cachot e pepe" mochi, prepared in the manner of a pepper and citrus risotto! He also has a penchant for less conventional ingredients, such as offal, which contribute unusual textures. Finally, another characteristic of his cuisine is the marriage of surf and turf, with dishes such as his superb black ruff, a fish from the Mediterranean seabed, judiciously combined with tripe and vin jaune. Over the course of a carte blanche menu that is unapologetically playful, a singular culinary personality emerges, shaking things up and winning diners over from start to finish.

Name: Koji
Description: Japanese teppanyaki cooking is nothing short of theatrical with its spectacular flames, so be sure to bag a front-row seat at the counter. Before your eyes, chef Koji Hashimoto carefully prepares premium ingredients. His elegant brand of craftsmanship, honed by years of experience in prestigious kitchens, never overwhelms the produce with culinary gimmicks. Both fish and meat (a Normandy beef fillet, for example) are cooked just right, and enhanced by impeccable sauces (eg white miso and sherry vinegar sauce on an assortment of grilled fish). Traditional Japanese decor dominated by wood.

Name: L'Unisens
Description: This modern building just outside the village of Vagnas harks back to traditional Provençal architecture. Its spacious interior, done out in a contemporary style with an open kitchen, is home to the new venture of Tarik Mezri-Charmasson. The chef (previously at Auberge des Granges in Bessas) still takes his cooking very seriously; his cuisine ticks all the boxes, remaining true to the seasons and letting the ingredients speak for themselves.

Name: Le Bruadan
Description: Jean-Charles Boulmier and Christelle Cauli (formerly of L'Épicurien) are clearly passionate about nature. Named in homage to the forest bordering the village where they have set up shop, their appealing modern restaurant has a decor with plenty of wooden features and a palette of green, as if better to evoke the region of Sologne. The chef, who has an impressive track record (L'Espérance with Marc Meneau, Le Grand Coeur in Méribel, La Villa in Calvi), follows the seasons closely with his mouth-watering dishes: fish mousse, mussels and pig's trotter; pork filet mignon, polenta and corn. A warm welcome and smiling service.

Name: TLALI
Description: This Franco-Mexican establishment run by a native of Guadalajara, chef Kristian de Anda who was at the helm of the kitchen of the Parisian Biondi, is a delightful surprise. Only open in the evenings, his establishment masterfully proves that there is more to Mexican cuisine than tacos and enchiladas! In fact, the score is more fusion as pedigree Gallic recipes are dotted with intelligent Mexican notes – you won’t find a single tastebud-burning pepper in sight! We do however recommend ordering his array of tacos, in tribute to different regions of Mexico, as the ideal appetiser to kick off your meal in style.

Name: Comptoir du Lac
Address: 410 allée de la Plage, Duingt, 74410, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: This restaurant looks like a modern industrial greenhouse and is surrounded by greenery, the mountains and a lake. A really lovely place that serves up dishes that are equally appealing!

Name: Auberge Bienvenue
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This place may have celebrated its 30th birthday but it shows no sign of tiring. Comfortably ensconced beneath the beams and arcades of the large dining area, you have to admit that at times nothing beats tradition, especially when it comes to cooking.

Name: Au Vieux Porche
Description: This typical residence (1707) stands in the winegrowing estate of the manager's family. His partner cooks classic regional dishes, but he is also a winemaker. So it goes without saying that you can enjoy some fine vintages here too.

Name: La Verdoyante
Description: Standing among the vines, this former rustic farmhouse enjoys a fine panoramic view... But La Verdoyante would be nothing without the enthusiasm of the couple who hold the reins. In the stylish interior or on the charming terrace, diners savour delicious Provençal cuisine that smacks of the garigue.

Name: Le Chalet
Description: A fortified house during the Middle Ages, and a monastery until 1905, this "chalet" is now a hotel and restaurant run by the Prayer family. The tasty dishes, such as house - smoked salmon or seven - hour leg of lamb with gratin du Vercors, attest to the two primordial values of the establishment: tradition and generosity.

Name: Le Cigalon
Description: This warm friendly eatery outside the village of Flayosc is run by a couple: she works front of house, while he crafts fine food: barigoule of fennel, olives, focaccia and squid; Mediterranean seabream, cranberry beans, courgettes and mussels; roast pear, star aniseed and hazelnut ice cream. The quintessence of the South of France.

Name: Le Carillon
Address: 10 avenue du Luberon (place de la Libération), Goult, 84220, France
Description: Facing the church on Goult's main square, this restaurant offers excellent Provençal-inspired cuisine with the odd contemporary twist. Tables are set up in a small dining area with modern decor and out on the terrace, where you can soak up the village atmosphere. A charming welcome and a well-devised wine list that pays particular attention to organic options. A lovely spot.

Name: Les Jardins Sauvages - La Grée des Landes
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: In the restaurant of the Yves Rocher hotel, chef Fabien Manzoni, a champion of vegetables, crafts modern, masterful and generous fare made with organic produce (except the seafood) from the garden and local growers. Vegetarians will be in Seventh Heaven, thanks to dishes such as pithivier of celeriac, Chioggia beetroot and lemon-flavoured spinach leaves with grated truffle and drizzled with truffle sauce.

Name: L'Un des Sens
Description: Near the antique dealers’ district, this restaurant serves scrumptious food, presented beautifully and rich in distinctive flavours, illustrated by a rack of Ségala veal, ravioles of green peas and pecorino cheese and spring onions. The vegetables and fruit come from the chef’s garden. Several-course surprise menu in the evening and simpler fare at lunchtime. Courtyard patio for alfresco dining.

Name: Les Santons
Description: This lovely Provençal inn is full of character, with its exposed beams, flower arrangements and, of course, its collection of figurines (santons in French). The menu never gets boring, alternating between classic cuisine and contemporary dishes, such as rack of lamb with crispy new garlic, garnished with a millefeuille of candied peppers and chard. The traditional aged-rum baba with vanilla whipped cream deserves a special mention.

Name: Le Pavillon Gourmand
Description: This village house (1683) offers a setting bathed in light, tastefully combining the historical character of the building with more contemporary touches. Tuck into cuisine that includes Alsace recipes (onion tart, sauerkraut, wild boar stew) and more modern dishes. Wines from the Eguisheim vineyard are well represented, and the small terrace is popular in summer.

Name: Les Gentianettes
Address: 73 route de Chevenne, La Chapelle-d'Abondance, 74360, France
Description: A mountain chalet decor with exposed beams, a traditional dining room with a fireplace in the middle and decorated with a collection of bells – it doesn't get much more inviting than this! The kitchen serves both traditional dishes, including beef tenderloin with a morel mushroom sauce, and slightly more modern and creative recipes such as carpaccio of sea bass with passion fruit. For Savoyard specialties, guests can head to La Baratte, the restaurant's ground-floor eatery, to tuck into authentic cuisine in a friendly atmosphere.

Name: L'Arbousier
Address: D55 - Boulevard Marie-Jeanne Bozzi, Porticcio, 20166, France
Description: A throwback to another time in this establishment with a slightly old-fashioned atmosphere, where Mediterranean cuisine with Corsican influences is served on the very pleasant terrace facing the sea. Lobster, fish from small-scale local fishermen… and fricassee of lobster with buttered capellini, the house speciality. The wine is served by the glass from magnums, which is a nice touch! More limited menu at lunchtime.

Name: La Taula Gallici
Address: Villa Gallici, 18 avenue de la Violette, Aix-en-Provence, 13100, France
Description: Luxury and tradition, with not a hint of ostentation... and far from the crowds, in the upper reaches of town. On the menu: good sun-drenched French cuisine to relish around the low tables of the superb lounges, or by the plane trees on the peaceful terrace. The chef's specialities include chilled lobster and gambero rosso bisque; vitello tonnato-style tortellini, ricotta, sun-dried tomatoes and taggiasche olives; "Gallici" tiramisu. The spirit of the South of France!

Name: La Bartavelle
Address: 24 rue de la République, Argelès-sur-Mer, 66700, France
Description: This place is an open secret among food lovers – and with good reason! Chef Thibaut Lesage and Stéphanie, his pastry chef wife, put an inspired spin on the classics to produce dishes that diners delight in. You will need to book ahead if you want to try it for yourself!

Name: La Poya
Description: In a mountain-inspired decor, the chef serves up good-quality traditional cuisine that often takes meat as its starting point… but does not exclude the odd Asian note (eg gravelax salmon tataki marinated in beetroot, served with mustard sorbet). The dishes are beautifully presented and service comes with a smile. A good place to recharge your batteries after hitting the slopes on your skis!

Name: À la 12
Address: 6 place de la République, Delme, 57590, France
Description: This has been the kingdom of the François family since it was founded in 1954. Thomas and Laura, the third generation at the helm, are upholding the family traditions. Thomas’ cuisine is simple only in appearance and quickly reveals subtlety and delicacy, with a distinct weakness for herbs and spices. Uplifting!

Name: La Gaffe
Description: Chef Yann Le Scavarec, who hails from Morbihan, is at the helm of this restaurant, which boasts an ideal location on the Saint-Florent harbour front. His well-crafted contemporary cooking showcases local produce, eg lamb and veal from Oletta, fish sourced directly from a local fisherman and barbecued crayfish. The grouper, courgette flower with spider crab and Vadouvan spices made an impression! The modern interior is in keeping with the menu.

Name: MaThy'S
Description: Picture a red façade preceded by a delightful patio shaded by a mulberry tree. On a street corner of Saint Florent, this eatery aims for a friendly village restaurant vibe and serves Mediterranean and Corsican cuisine (carpaccio of langoustines, olive oil and dried caviar, tartare of red tuna or grilled squid with chorizo), without forgetting a few more exotic Asian notes (yuzu-flavoured gyoza or crunchy king prawns, nori and wasabi). Simpler lunchtime menu and a highly tempting wine list add the final touch to this inviting portrait.

Name: La Table de Courcelles - Château de Courcelles
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: This 17C ‘Grand Siècle’ edifice and its Second Empire-inspired Winter Garden are the quintessence of style. The fashionably modern recipes are paired with an impressive wine list. We tasted lightly seared foie gras; guinea fowl from “L’Ourcq” farm, cooked two ways, with confit of leeks, morels and a champagne sauce and confit of rhubarb and Kayambe ivory chocolate to finish. The good life!

Name: La Table de la Grotte
Address: Domaine de Murtoli, Vallée de l'Ortolo, Sartène, 20100, France
Description: Above the Domaine de Murtoli golf course, set deep in the maquis, this restaurant charms diners with its absolutely unique location and its delicious and flavoursome cuisine, which features quality ingredients either from the estate itself or sourced from neighbouring producers. On wooden benches nestled among the rock formations, or on one of the superb little terraces with a splendid view, you dine by romantic candlelight, tucking into typical Corsican dishes that take the form of a single set menu: courgette à la Sartenaise, confit shoulder of lamb... and a tomato sauce with herbs from the maquis that in itself is worth the trip. Booking essential.

Name: Les Orfèvres
Description: Bang in the middle of town, this restaurant sports a modern, pared-down, workshop interior and a friendly vibe. The menu is no stranger to the classics, albeit with the odd more modern touch. The chef avows a weakness for fish, illustrated by his superlative low-temperature loin of cod, honey-flavoured fermented milk, leeks and celery.

Name: Le 59 Restaurant
Description: This restaurant is a family affair for the Campanellas, with Cédric having taken over from his brother Boris at the reins of this converted grocer's shop. The cuisine demonstrates a sense of precision, and comprises modern, ever-inventive dishes. One of the best spots in town.

Name: La Cigogne
Description: Not far from Angoulême, La Cigogne is located at the foot of old stone quarries – a rather unusual location, to be sure. Elegant contemporary setting, verdant terrace, and fresh cuisine prepared with good local ingredients.

Name: L'Aubergade
Description: Chef Éric Boutté, a fine connoisseur of local Picardy produce and sometime globetrotter, makes classically inspired cuisine that is in tune with the seasons and made with the best the market has to offer. The elegant dining area has an appealingly restrained decor. Don't leave without tasting the house special of stuffed cabbage: over 20 000 have already been served!

Name: Grand Largue
Description: From the upper floor of this villa, diners enjoy fine views over the gulf of Morbihan and gastronomic seafood cuisine (lobster, sea bass, shellfish). On the ground floor, the P'tit Zeph is a bistro with a distinctly seafaring air.

Name: Tempi Fà
Description: Welcome to "bygone days" (tempi fà), in this grocer's-cum-bistro run by a passionate man who selects the island's finest ingredients! You enter via the shop, reminiscent of an actual village market (cold cuts, cheeses, myrtle liqueur etc). You'll enjoy tucking into the tender, flavoursome Abbatucci veal chop with a jus flavoured with herbs from the maquis... and a fine wine from the island!

Name: Les Cornettes
Address: 43 route des Frasses, La Chapelle-d'Abondance, 74360, France
Description: This restaurant, listed in the Michelin Guide since 1933, is a real institution, renowned throughout the Chablais region. On the menu: game pie, lake trout fillet with wild garlic and morels, guinea fowl roasted on the bone. The cold cuts are matured and smoked on site in a typical mountain atmosphere. It's simple, tasty and rustic as can be.

Name: Cuq en Terrasses
FacilitiesAndServices: Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: High up in the village, this charming 18C house is a haven of calm. It boasts an unusual terraced garden and extends a warm family welcome. The chef, originally from the Cyclades, showcases vegetables from the kitchen garden and Mediterranean cuisine. A breathtaking view of the Lauragais plain and the Pyrenees can be enjoyed from the verandah and terrace in clear weather. The (musical) icing on the cake: the chef regales diners with a player piano piece at the end of the meal.

Name: L'Attilio - Château de Noirieux
Address: Château de Noirieux, 26 route du Moulin, Briollay, 49125, France
Description: This handsome little 17C château and charming 15C manor house are set in grounds on the banks of the River Loir. The elegant dining room and pleasant terrace overlooking the valley set the scene for the new chef's modernised cuisine. He chooses quality ingredients and delivers technically sound dishes, which can be accompanied by fine wines (the wine list is, for the most part, devoted to regional tipples).

Name: Comte Roger
Description: This restaurant within the medieval city walls has a sleek contemporary design and tables set up on a lovely airy patio – Comte Roger knows how to welcome guests! Cassoulet (the house speciality) is of course given pride of place, along with seasonal and regional ingredients (asparagus and local lamb, Lauragais lentils, Belpech poultry etc), which are prepared with a keen sense of precision.

Name: Auberge Larochette
Description: This pleasant village inn serves hearty traditional cuisine, such as a fine Charolais entrecôte with gratin dauphinois, or crispy calf sweetbreads. As for dessert, the hot soufflé with praline, walnuts and pear is nicely done. In winter the fire crackles in the hearth; in summer the shady terrace is the place to be. Attentive front-of-house staff.

Name: Le 1131 - Abbaye de la Bussière
Description: It would be hard to imagine a more inspiring place in which to conjure up such refined cuisine than a 12C Cistercian abbey. Beneath these impressive ribbed vaults, a wonderful tribute is paid to the terroir of Burgundy (snails, frog legs, lake and river fish, blackcurrants and honey from the flowers growing in the gardens), not to mention a wine list that harbours many treasures. Prolong the meditative experience in the 7ha grounds. Luxurious guestrooms are also available.

Name: Le Shardana
Address: 16 rue de la République, Bandol, 83150, France
Description: Bang in the middle of the seaside resort, this spruce, modern edifice is reminiscent of Sardinia, both in terms of the décor and the succulent seasonal food. The menu, which changes monthly, is liberally strewn with local and Sardinian ingredients. Examples include gently steamed local croaker in a tomato and cognac sauce with crunchy vegetables and black garlic or panettone French toast with roast apples, salted butterscotch and a scoop of stracciatella ice cream. The chef’s radiant wife cheerfully and professionally manages the front of house. Concise wine list of mainly Italian and local vintages.

Name: La Brasserie du Corton
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The brasserie offshoot of Villa Madie continues to foster simplicity with its market-fresh ingredients and enticing surf and turf combinations. The set menus are different at lunch and dinner, as well as being changed on a weekly basis. Less expensive than at the original restaurant, the dishes here are just as tasty (beef tartare with Tamaris oysters, real Marseille sôcisse with fennel, lemon tart. When the weather is fine, head for the terrace, which commands a knockout view of the pretty bay.

Name: Le Bellevue
Description: The interior is light, and the menu is short. Two reasons to linger in this tastefully decorated restaurant. Traditional cuisine is revisited with enthusiasm and a keen sense of the pleasure of food. Try off - the - bone pig's trotter terrine or, for dessert, the hot soufflé with pear brandy.

Name: Maison Demarcq
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This grand town house close to where the famous Treaty of Cambrai is said to have been signed (1529) has gone down in history for hosting Napoleon. The decor fosters classical elegance, and the food is contemporary and meticulous – a good option in the town renowned for its "Bêtises de Cambrai" sweets. The simpler traditional cuisine served at the brasserie L'Éphémère is an alternative option.

Name: La Sittelle
Description: This inviting late-1940’s villa is enjoying a new lease of life thanks to two associates, formerly of Locguénolé chateau. The chef enhances regional produce in recipes with a creative twist, displaying a preference for surf and turf dishes. Welcoming and attentive service.

Name: Auberge de la Forêt
Address: 276 rue des Verriers, à Lettenbach, Abreschviller, 57560, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This turreted inn is nestled in the Abreschviller valley. Gone are any airs of a country bistro; the style is now up to the minute, elegant and refined, in line with the food, which is very contemporary.

Name: Les 3 Lieux - La Table
Description: In this restaurant on the banks of the Loire River, diners enjoy the chef's creative, spirited cuisine, which is proposed as a three- to seven-course menu-carte. Try, for example, the superb blanquette of sweetbreads with a twist, but also the foie gras, cocoa and orange, and a dessert of chocolate, hazelnut and thyme mousse. Meticulously and deftly made.

Name: Notes de Saveurs
Description: Sitting in the vaulted room with exposed stones, looking onto the ruins of the former Benedictine convent, you can enjoy food that places the onus on quality ingredients. The dishes are generous, delicious, flavoursome and original. A friendly and pleasant place, opened by a young couple in 2011.

Name: Mâche
Description: Butternut, carrot and haddock in shades of orange; a gutsy duet of squab and asparagus, both crunchy and tender. The inventive cuisine of Michaël Gamet (with a stint at l’Astrance) is a culinary festival of taste, colour and flavour that packs a punch (of which fermented and confit ingredients and powerful seasonings are the stars) and is dotted with souvenirs of the chef’s travels and culinary encounters. The handsome interior mingles vintage details with contemporary geometric design features, while an upbeat vibe and a friendly team set the scene for the front-of-house service.

Name: Chez Jules Le Don Juan
Description: The major appeal of this particular Don Juan is its enthusiastic, hardworking owner-chef, who tirelessly sources produce (vegetables from his family, veal from an Aveyron farm etc). His food is steeped in the flavours of Provence and Nice cuisine: house specialties are pissaladière, petits farcis niçois, gnocchi à la daube and aioli. The restaurant is part of a convivial little hub for gourmets, complete with café, grocery shop and bistro. Atmosphere guaranteed.

Name: L'Assierois
Description: In the village centre, opposite the church, this former inn with a pleasant shady terrace now presents a sleek contemporary interior. The chef proposes fairly simple seasonal cooking on weekday lunchtimes, and much more ambitious dishes in the evening and at weekends, but he always takes care to maximise local ingredients.

Name: La Cuisine
Description: In the centre of this town, “la cuisine” is well and truly honoured in this excellent eatery. Chef Johann Dubernet, assisted in the dining room by cheerful Isabelle, his partner, signs colourful, fragrant and beautifully presented dishes whose influences are manifold: tempura of frog’s legs in curry and saté sauce; John Dory in a green tomato and shiso leaf chutney; brownie with pineapple poached in combava and a spicy sorbet. Subtle, suave, spot-on cooking!

Name: Château de Salettes
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This restaurant enjoys a prime location: a 13C château in the heart of a Gaillac wine estate. The food, very much in tune with the zeitgeist, is based on fine ingredients and the attractive wine list proposes Château de Salettes wines. On fine days, the terrace oozes with charm, as do the contemporary-furnished guestrooms and suites established in the edifice’s historic towers and the surrounding wall.

Name: Ryoko - Comptoir à ramen
Address: 14 rue de la Fontaine, Vannes, 56000, France
Description: The flavoursome codes of Japanese cuisine are now part and parcel of French dining habits. This pocket handkerchief bistro embodies this trend, depicted by a red, white and black façade. You will taste one of the best ramens in town, based on pork (tonkotsu) or chicken (Tori chintan) broth – it’s your choice! Made with first-class local ingredients (pigs fed on flax seed), each dish is a masterpiece of Japanese tradition. A word of warning: they don’t accept bookings and the place is often packed to the seams!

Name: Hyacinthe
Description: Previously active in the humanitarian sector, this chef found a new calling while being trained by mentors such as Cyril Lignac and Hélène Darroze. Remaining true to his ethos here in his vintage restaurant, he is mindful of the relationship between his cooking, nature and people, sourcing vegetables from the Hortillonnages (cultivated islets in Amiens), saltmarsh lamb from the Baie de Somme estuary, line-caught fish from the Côte d'Opale etc. Filet mignon pie, vegetable pickles or monkfish, tomato, aubergine and sea herbs: his – at times creative – dishes draw on various preparation techniques, good ingredients and flavours.

Name: Le Baron
Description: Le Baron is the fine dining restaurant of the Château de Ferrières, located in the heart of the former Rothschild residence, which has become a prestigious hotel management school. Here, you can relish cuisine based on classical principles in a unique and sumptuous setting.

Name: Jeu de Quilles
Description: Iced courgette velouté with mint and burrata, or grilled Aubrac beef with smoked pepper: the chef of this tiny bistro proposes simple and appetising market-based cuisine. The very reasonably priced dishes are listed on the blackboard. Don't miss the pleasant terrace under the arbour.

Name: Prélude
Description: Far more than a prelude, this is a full-blown symphony! Now established in a spruce traditional building, Élodie Ouchelli and Thibault Étienne practiced their scales in top star restaurants, among which that of Romuald Fassenet. The virtuoso chef, whose talent is a masterclass in culinary subtlety, composes harmonious dishes in which first-class local produce plays the leading role. Several tables of the contemporary dining room provide a view of the chef at work in the kitchen.

Name: Le Petit Jardin - La Chenevière
Description: The Château de la Chenevière bistro is housed in the old orangery and has retained its large glass roof. Nestled between the garden and the swimming pool, it is decorated in a charming "English cottage" style. Tuck into good seasonal bistronomy fare: low temperature egg, cream of celery, cockles, samphire and wholegrain mustard; goat cheese risotto, snow peas, mushrooms and garlic cream.

Name: Onaka
Description: Tucked away in a cul-de-sac, this sushi bar is invariably packed to the seams (booking highly recommended). The chef at the helm, sushi champion of France, trained in several of chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s establishments, no less. Impeccably cooked rice, moist tender chicken, melt-in-the-mouth salmon, juicy red tuna, firm seabass, spicy miso sauce dusted with fresh garden herbs, last-minute grated wasabi and a knockout selection of sakés (the sommelier and partner knows his business). The omakase menu features a festival of flavours for a fine dining experience that can be adapted to suit the appetites and wallets of everyone.

Name: L'Estran
Description: Roasted green asparagus, lardo di Colonnata, bear's garlic foam; œuf parfait ("perfectly cooked egg"), creamy mushrooms with truffles, crispy foie gras, oyster mushrooms; line-caught pollack, fregola sarda, spring onions… In this compact restaurant by the quayside, chef Xavier Audren pursues his passion for bistronomy that takes its cue from the seasons and the fish market a few blocks away. On top of all that, the first set menu is very reasonably priced.

Name: La Plancha
Description: This place may be discreet, but its original menu makes it well worth coming for a meal here. The dishes are simple, effective and occasionally creative; the flavours are striking, eg Iberico pork belly with peas, bacon and horseradish. Special mentions have to go to the punchy bulli dog sauce and the profiteroles, which are made in time-honoured tradition.

Name: Le M
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Plenty of originality in the design of the dishes and the marriages of flavours in this typically Breton granite house done out with a contemporary decor. Tuck into modern cuisine that sources its ingredients (fish, poultry, vegetables etc) from local producers. In summer, dine alfresco on the pleasant terrace.

Name: 16âme
Address: 32 rue des Glaciers, Le Monêtier-les-Bains, 05220, France
Description: Behind a discreet façade is this inviting restaurant with decor that calls to mind a trapper's hut – we are in the mountains, after all! Julien Momon, originally from Corsica, worked in the kitchens of Christophe Bacquié and Gérard Boyer (formerly chef at Les Crayères in Reims) before becoming head chef at a hotel here in Monêtier-les-Bains. His dishes contain nothing but seasonal and local ingredients from this rural and Alpine territory, such as lamb from the Hautes-Alpes, coriander, mint, a pearly jus with olive oil or his lovage-infused cream.

Name: Taokan
Description: Come inside this pretty restaurant in the heart of St-Germain-des-Prés to enjoy light and fragrant Cantonese cuisine, with a few detours to the territory of Southeast Asia: the obligatory dim sum, steamed fish, spicy beef or lok lak. Lovely presentation and good ingredients: a real ambassador for Chinese food.

Name: Prosper
Description: When a winemaker from the Côte de Beaune meets a starred chef, you get Prosper! This lovely contemporary bistro in the Château St Aubin is the result of a collaboration between the Prosper Maufoux wine estate and the restaurateur Édouard Mignot (restaurant Ed.Em in Chassagne-Montrachet). The chef proposes a menu inspired by the Burgundy terroir. Pleasant terrace with a view of the vineyards.

Name: Les Parisiens
Description: Inside a new luxury hotel located in Faubourg-Saint-Germain, this restaurant adopts all the codes of the luxury brasserie genre. Wood panelling, large mirrors, mosaic floors, velvet banquettes, gilding, black marble tables: it is elegant, slightly retro and very cosy – a winning formula. Curated by Thibault Sombardier, the menu represents a refreshed and updated take on tradition. A fine and eclectic wine list, complete with some great bottles.

Name: Milagro
Description: An American chef who was born in New Mexico, Justin Kent honed his skills with the likes of Alain Passard and David Toutain. His dinky neo-vintage bistro couldn’t be more bang on: white marble and oak counter, parquet floor, light wooden tables, vintage green velvet wooden armchairs. International and Parisian bistronomic influences happily rub shoulders in the kitchen: fritters of chorizo and sweet potatoes, Greek yoghurt; lamb chops, emulsion of sweetcorn, risotto of spelt; creamy delight of celeriac with white chocolate, ice cream and meringues.

Name: Magma
Description: Like magma, Japanese chef Ryuya Ono (former second of Table) fusions French haute cuisine with his own constantly renewed inspiration and gourmet instincts. The result is a menu that can change daily. His signature dessert, meringue filled with cherry tomatoes and vine peach sorbet, is a gourmet gem of fiendish appeal. A black and white tiled floor, olive green bench seating, modern wooden furniture, a mirror and a vintage bar paint the inviting picture.

Name: So'Mets
Description: After honing her skills in top restaurants (including La Vague d’Or), chef Anne-Sophie Sabini has struck out on her own in this modern, colourful gastropub, flanked by a lovely terrace. She has devised a concise menu that changes monthly, in which she adds a feminine, modern touch to Gallic standards: cream of green peas with a 64° poached egg, coppa, crunchy croutons and organic olive oil from Provence; roast squid and black pudding, purée of carrots, citrus-flavoured dressing; sorbet of Beaulieu mandarin, anis-flavoured biscuit, praline and drizzled citrus fruit and bergamot … Slick service, charming welcome. Heaven for foodies!

Name: Patachée
Description: This small traditional restaurant in the town centre sports a bistro vibe, while rustic touches bear witness to the establishment’s age. The seasoned chef concocts tasty dishes with what his suppliers bring in fresh daily in a modern, hearty vein in which spices are often cast in the leading role: raviole of squab in Thai stock; lobster and cockles in curry-flavoured court-bouillon or line-caught pollock with an emulsion of Hanoi spices. Lunchtime menu at prices that make sense.

Name: Garenne
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Wheelchair access
Description: In a landscape of hills and vineyards in Drôme Provençale, the farmhouse on this small organic winegrowing estate has been restored and is now home to a hotel and a fine dining restaurant. The lovely, bright contemporary space (almost a veranda with its open sides) allows you to feast on the surrounding nature, too. Artichoke and creamed artichoke accompanied by a surprising oyster ice cream; sole garnished with dulse seaweed, white asparagus caramelised and in an emulsion, shredded bottarga and confit shallot purée: local and organic produce, the plating, jus and sauces all appeal to the taste buds! A charming welcome and professional service.

Name: Black Bass
Address: Black Bass Hotel, 921 route d'Albertville, à Sevrier, Annecy, 74000, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: A smart vibe, a hip interior and a sweeping view of the lake set the scene for bistronomic recipes scattered with creative, exotic accents: ceviche of croaker with coriander and jalapenos; barbecued organic seabass with a harissa of raspberries and salad of green beans; spaghetti with toasted breadcrumbs, lemon and basil…

Name: POF
Description: The lunchtime menu is chalked up on a slate, while in the evening, the dishes of the concise menu carry playful, tongue-in-cheek names, which do however require a certain command of the French language to be appreciated! The globetrotting partners aim for a friendly vibe, a wide range of culinary influences (cream of cauliflower with Brittany curry spices, wakame crumble; crunchy quinoa and a Mexican-inspired jus; pear, myrtle, star anis, mascarpone and matcha tea) and market-fresh ingredients in line with the zeitgeist.

Name: Ezkia
Address: 6 avenue de la Grande-Plage, Bidart, 64210, France
Description: Whether beneath the lime trees (ezkia in Basque) on the terrace, or inside the small, inviting and intimate restaurant room with exposed stonework, floorboards, saffron-coloured velvet seats and banquettes, it is the same traditional Basque house. Standing in the heart of the delightful village of Bidart, it exudes a quiet, refined atmosphere. The couple who run the place, defectors from Michel Guérard's restaurant, serve nice seasonal precisely cooked dishes, full of good local Basque produce e.g. farm-reared pig, line-caught tuna, black cherry, mature farm cheeses.

Name: Patern
Description: This magnificently located eatery is only a 5-minute walk from Stanislas Square! The youthful owner-chef, Martin Debuiche, former deputy of Jean-Pierre Vigato of the Apicius in Paris, has teamed up with a butcher-breeder, Alexandre Polmard. In a smart, modern interior, he crafts surprise menus based on flawlessly sourced fine ingredients: fish from Brittany, Vosges pigeon, dairy produce from Meurthe-et-Moselle, saffron from Lorraine, etc. Examples include Brittany John Dory, savory, fennel and girolles, or pigeon, foie gras, lardo di Colonnata and spinach.

Name: Eunoé
Description: Japanese chef Ryuji Sato and Félix Perotte (front of house) are two friends who are passionate about food and wine. They offer hospitality at this location near Square Maurice Gardette. In a modern, stylishly "unfinished" setting in sand and ochre tones, the chef delivers his fine, no-holds-barred take on the culinary zeitgeist, with an emphasis on flavour in every dish: pork loin soaked in its full-bodied jus with aged sherry vinegar and a hint of thyme, smoked potato mash and a small salad of fresh herbs, seasoned to perfection. At dinner, the elegance goes up a notch.

Name: Benjamin Schmitt Restaurant
Description: In the heart of Pigalle, this eatery pays tribute to the land and those who work it. The youthful chef cultivates culinary eclecticism, seamlessly segueing from one style of cuisine to another and from traditional to modern. The enticing names of the dishes live up to their promise: duck, foie gras and pork pâté en croûte; veal breast confit with olives, aubergine and anchovies; strawberry and rhubarb pavlova... Sensibly priced lunch menu, tasting and à la carte menus in the evening.

Name: Le France
FacilitiesAndServices: Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Between Morteau and La Chaux-de-Fonds, not far from the French-Swiss border, this restaurant welcomes guests to the heart of the Haut-Doubs mountains. In this family-run place, chef Hugues Droz offers guests typical Franche-Comté hospitality, just as his father and grandfather did before him. With a keen eye on seasonal produce, he loves to ally terroir and innovation. He also enjoys creating themed meals, such as his morel-based menu, in which this mushroom features in every course.

Name: Alluma
Description: Former Balagan chef Liran Tal has tastefully revamped this establishment with immaculate white walls. He crafts delicious Mediterranean cuisine with Israeli influences, served in the form of tasting menus that are very good value for money: delicious msabbaha hummus, yellowtail crudo with figs and spices, lamb sirloin and an apricot-miso condiment. Choice of organic and biodynamic wines, most notably from Italy, Spain and Armenia.

Name: La Dariole
Description: In the heart of the old town and not far from the cathedral, this 15C half-timbered house showcases an easy alliance of old stonework and cosy touches. The chef, who even trained here when he was learning his trade, hits the mark with delicious cuisine that is in tune with the times. The seasonal menu changes regularly and features appealingly tasty dishes such as pork chop with potatoes and a caper jus.

Name: Kazumi
Description: Behind the discreet façade of this Japanese restaurant, chef Kazumi Hatakenaka is at work. Having first come to France to open a traditional French restaurant in the Beaujolais region, he is now serving cuisine that speaks to his dual culinary culture (French and Japanese). His tasting menu alternates French classic and dishes with ingredients prepared on the teppanyaki – with characteristic Japanese finesse and touches. Fresh produce (fish, meat and vegetables), mouth-watering dishes such as scallops, pak choi and shiitake, cooking and seasonings that are on point make for a delightful culinary escapade. For dinner, allow three hours at your table.

Name: Castel Ac'h
Description: Brittany is full of magical places and the Abers region is one such! Just a stone’s throw from the lighthouses of Ile Vierge and Ile de Wrac’h, this handsome neo-Brittany house enjoys a superb location opposite the picturesque Lilia Beach. The food is of regional inspiration with a range of tasty surf and turf ingredients and the lunchtime menu is a steal. In the evening, two set menus and one à la carte play a bistronomic Brittany score (oysters, abalone, fish of the day, veggies from the cottage garden, seaweed and sarrazin wheat). The spacious dining room sports a minimalist vibe with white walls and a terrace.

Name: Les Roseaux Pensants
Description: This quaint historic village is the lair of a self-taught couple, who sources their organic ingredients entirely locally thus enabling them to develop close ties with the producers in person. The gutsy result demonstrates a weakness for veggies and fermentation illustrated by vegetarian black pudding paired with confit of apple and black garlic, although the menu does feature a sprinkling of meat and fish dishes. The chef, who practised law before he fell in love with cooking, rustles up heroically wondrous food such as barbecued breast of guinea fowl, roast courgettes and aubergines, scrumptious aïoli and peach-pepper pickles for a final spicy kick. A delightful patio shaded by linden trees in fine weather and swish, slick service.

Name: À l'Échevin
Description: In the heart of “Little Venice”, the half-timbered Le Maréchal hotel is home to a comfortable and classically-decorated restaurant. The food is rather more adventurous and the chef deftly crafts modern recipes, putting a new spin on regional and gastronomic favourites, thanks to a sprinkling of creative touches. Delicious desserts, like this duo of figs and creamed rice in a crisp cinnamon-scented tuile. We recommend booking a seat in the blue dining room which overlooks the Lauch River.

Name: La Cotriade
Description: On the quayside, facing the fishing port, the ice buffet bar with its array of fish and shellfish sits majestically in front of the restaurant. The atmosphere inside is, naturally, a seaside one, and the chef can be seen at work in his open kitchen. The menu features seafood platters, fresh fish advertised on the daily specials board, some rather traditional dishes and specialities such as the royal sea bream cooked in a banana leaf, lime and coconut milk, the whole sea bass roasted with fennel and flambéed with aniseed, or the famous cotriade – Brittany's answer to bouillabaisse. There are also some meat dishes.

Name: Saba
Description: There is no shortage of Japanese chefs mad about French food, but here is a French chef who is crazy about Japanese cuisine, which he showcases beautifully in his tiny restaurant in historic Annecy. His freshly-sourced, vibrant dishes hit the spot every time: gyozas of smoked eel and saba (mackerel in Japanese); koshihikari rice, giant prawns and curry… All of which in line with a sustainable agriculture and fishing ethos. Cheerful service.

Name: L'Altiplano au K2 Palace
Address: Le K2 Palace, 238 rue des Clarines, Courchevel 1850, Courchevel, 73120, France
Description: At this high altitude restaurant with a cosy and intimate interior, ceviche classico of white fish marinated in tiger's milk; grilled prawns, spring onion, red pepper and lime; and postre estilo pisco are just some of the (delicious) examples of the modernised Peruvian food you can tuck into – think tasty, colourful and spicy with a delicate touch.

Name: Oktobre
Description: In one of the most bookish streets of the scholarly St André des Arts neighbourhood, Oktobre is warm and welcoming, like an Indian summer. The chef's pantry is stocked with only the finest, painstakingly sourced produce (he buys some animals whole). He takes a fresh, delicate, natural approach to cooking, deftly seasoning his dishes with varied spices and Asian accents. “Dentelles de Cucugnan” cuttlefish pasta with a shellfish bisque; Dombes quail, buckwheat risotto with mushrooms, fig and gochujang pickles; figs topped with a shiso-scented diplomat cream…

Name: L'Ancienne Auberge
Description: This establishment is in a former lemonade factory. The nostalgic 1940s bistro decor pays tribute to the inn opened by the Blanc family in the late 19C (old photos and posters). Regional cuisine.

Name: ROS[O]
Description: The name is a play on words referring to the reeds (roseaux) on the banks of the Louet, overlooked by this restaurant's delightful terrace. Quail eggs, Comté cheese and courgettes make for a fresh, well-seasoned dish; tender Duroc pork chop cooked rare, served with Noirmoutier new potatoes and vegetables – chef Tony Pasquier (formerly of Casa Corneille in the centre of Angers) knows the ingredients and the seasons inside out. He has a knack for coming up with mouth-watering dishes for you to enjoy in this bright, modern space.

Name: Le P'tit Bateau
Description: In the heart of the medieval city, Le P'tit Bateau sets out to tantalise our taste buds with fresh produce, including fish sourced directly from Brittany's fish markets, as well as game from Sologne in season. The dishes are generous, precise, carefully presented and tasty. It is worth noting there is a pleasant patio for a meal al fresco. An eatery committed to doing a good job.

Name: Le Restaurant 1451
Description: Imagine an old stone house with splashes of midnight blue and a modern, elegant interior flanked by a lovely courtyard terrace. The scene is set for a fine dining experience. The chef crafts fresh, modern recipes in which artistically displayed vegetables are often cast in the lead roles: snails with garden tomatoes and herbs; red mullet, fennel and orange; strawberries with unpasteurised cream and marigolds.

Name: Lacertus
Description: Good-humoured staff, friendly service, a convivial atmosphere, modern cuisine with a touch of inventiveness (eg fish sausage or a seaweed/mustard sorbet as part of the mackerel starter; a lime/pea sorbet alongside a chocolate dessert), quality local produce and a few ingredients gathered wild (mustard seeds): this is the winning formula behind this small restaurant a stone's throw from Le Remblai promenade. In case you were wondering, the name Lacertus means "mackerel" in Latin.

Name: La Conciergerie
Address: 4405 rue de la Lys, Sailly-sur-la-Lys, 62840, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The former concierge lodge in the grounds of the Château de Bac-Saint-Maur is now home to this modern restaurant. Bathed in light thanks to its large bay windows, the space features a few design details that reflect the season. Langoustine and beetroot for starters; veal, mussels and samphire for the main course; tomato, vanilla zephyr and oregano ice cream for dessert: the chef aims to surprise with cuisine that is creative (in moderation), and made with good ingredients, mainly local and seasonal.

Name: Les Allées
Description: Antoine and Coralie met in Jean Cousseau's two-Michelin-starred restaurant (Relais de la Poste in Magescq) after gaining solid experience in France and Spain. This former café-restaurant has been given a facelift that subtly blends vintage and modern features (waxed concrete floors paired with exposed beams). As for the food, this pair of pros focuses on flavour, often drawing on the Iberian pantry to put a spin on traditional dishes: calf's head croquette; leeks in vinaigrette; sautéed sweetbreads; grilled octopus etc. Two terraces: one out front and one in the courtyard, away from the street.

Name: Sharmaji
Description: At the helm of several establishments, Manoj Sharma has boldly set about freeing Indian food from its hackneyed clichés (like the predictable tandoori or korma chicken). In a spruce, modern, colourful venue, his authentic bistronomic cooking delves into an Indian score that has shaken off its traditional visual and technical fetters. Examples include masala fried chicken, with coconut and curry leaves; long sweet peppers stuffed with masala cheese and yoghurt sauce; caramelised ginger cake. Simmered and crafted with lashings of spices and aromatic herbs, Manoj’s delicious dishes nonetheless find favour with delicate western palates. The lunch menu is a bargain. The à la carte menu changes regularly.

Name: La fleur de Sel
Description: The initiative by this pair, chef Willy Lardry and maître d' Edwin Smietanski, to open their restaurant here is most welcome. Both hail from Le Creusot but met while working for Yohann Chapuis in Tournus. The interior is inspired in part by nature (with, in particular, wallpaper depicting a forest in the mist). The chef, working alone in the kitchen, shows undeniable maturity. Delicacy and finesse are the order of the day, for example, the lovely courgette flower with cod stuffing and the olive oil sabayon accompanying the cod tournedos, or the mackerel and its marinated cucumber ravioli.

Name: Le Bistrot de Cancale
Address: à Port-Mer, 5 rue Eugène-et-Auguste-Feyen, Cancale, 35260, France
Description: Run by Hugo Roellinger, this restaurant is located opposite the beach at Port-Mer with its small boats bobbing at anchor and Mont-Saint-Michel visible in the distance. The menu features dishes such as oysters, shellfish, langoustines, sole with a caramelised jus, turbot cooked on the bone, lobster cooked over hot coals – excellent fish, distinguished by its remarkable freshness and often seasoned with Olivier Roellinger's famous spice mixes. There is a beautiful terrace with a sea view and, inside, knick-knacks related to Brittany and fishing create a chic and modernised seaside bistro vibe that is enhanced by a 1930s fresco depicting a scene from life in the port of Saint-Malo.

Name: Sillon
Description: In a quiet little street in the city centre, chef Mathieu Rostaing-Tayard, with spells in the kitchens of Pierre Gagnaire, Michel Portos, Massimo Bottura and even Virgilio Martinez in Peru under his belt, runs this stylish, pared-down venue. It features two culinary vibes: a counter at the entrance serving tapas-style dishes to share, or the quieter dining room with a tasting menu starring top-drawer Basque ingredients (line-caught hake, turbot, Basque pork). In both cases, the chef's creative cuisine hits the spot every time thanks to wholehearted, authentic flavours, without forgetting the elegant plating.

Name: L'Ouzeri
Description: Saganaki cheese, gyro merida, myzithropita (cheesecake), spanakopita – the menu gives it away: this is French-Greek chef Mikaela Liaroutsos's new Greek taverna, and it's just a stone's throw from the original restaurant that made her name. The food is served as a series of mezes, to savour as you dream of Greek holidays, past or future. The traditional songs playing in the background might tempt you to pull out a sirtaki step after a glass of ouzo.

Name: La Cage aux Fleurs
Description: Flowers and colours abound in this spruce-looking bistro, both in the decor (floral wallpaper, varnished porcelain knick-knacks) and on the plate: tuna tartare, pumpkin seeds, grilled butternut condiment, anchovies with green pepper; roast fillet of sea bass, panisse (chickpea fries), saffron, fennel. This cuisine in tune with the zeitgeist is delivered by a professional couple – themselves the offspring of restaurant owners – who work in tandem. French classics that are the winegrowers' favourites and cuts of meat to share are also present and correct.

Name: La Colombe
Description: At the foot of Mont Ventoux surrounded by vineyards, this gourmet dove coos a delicious melody. Chef Christophe Schuffenecker (formerly of the star-rated Château de Mazan) serves modern, spot-on dishes, blessedly free of superfluous extras, such as Sarrians pigeon with geranium-perfumed mashed carrots. When the weather is fine, make a beeline for the terrace shaded by awnings overlooking the vineyards. The stylish interior sports bare beams and a large Provençal fireplace, as well as a permanent art exhibition.

Name: L'Embarcadère
Address: 15 avenue de la Plage, Jassans-Riottier, 01480, France
Description: Georges Blanc's new restaurant, on the banks of the Saône, is a cross between a chic guinguette and a contemporary brasserie. The food is traditional but trendy with dishes like frogs' legs, poached free - range egg with whiting, and Bresse chicken.

Name: La Mère Germaine
