The chic glass-fronted kitchen turns out dishes made from high-quality ingredients that are for the most part sourced in the region and are meticulously prepared by means of traditional methods. The list of French and Swiss wines rounds it all off. The service is efficient and professional yet far from stuffy.

Name: Käserei
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Wheelchair access
Description: This restaurant with a modern yet rustic feel and a cosy atmosphere is located in the former cowshed of a typical Engadin house. The restaurant still has a focus on cows and dairy products today, serving dishes such as cheese fondues, raclette, capuns and even Chinese fondue. Cheese-making demonstrations are held regularly in the evenings.

Name: Le Cerf
Description: This century-old culinary institution is a renowned name in the region. Reinvented from top to bottom, it now serves good old unpretentious dishes in a traditional vein: for example, strips of veal from the Pays d'Enhaut, golden rösti and green salad… and let's not forget the malakoffs – fried cheese balls made with PDO cheese from the old fort in the valley – and the fondues! Cosy, rustic-style ambience, plus a superb terrace with mountain views.

Name: Rechberg 1837
Description: The Rechberg 1837 is a pleasant restaurant with a unique philosophy – it only uses regional produce that was available around 1837 (the year the house was built), i. e. before industrialisation. Innovative dishes such as slices of country pork on pea puree with fried barley and pickled onion are served in the evening, with a more traditional selection available at lunchtime. Cosy atmosphere and charming service.

Name: Le Monument
Description: In this welcoming and well-maintained auberge near the church in the centre of the village, the kitchen team has mastered the classics (the different tartare dishes on the menu are particularly memorable!) as highlighted in cuisine that showcases subtle Italian influences. Recommended.

Name: Bad Schauenburg
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Whether you're seated in the Basler Stübli, the Gaststube or the Veranda, the fine dining restaurant of Hotel Bad Schauenburg serves classic French cuisine that takes its cue from the seasons in all its lovely rooms. Some of the produce comes from the hotel's own garden. The highlight in summer is of course the delightful terrace!

Name: Le Roc
Description: The restaurant of the Hôtel de Rougemont serves classic French cuisine with a contemporary twist. The house-smoked salmon, green asparagus in breadcrumbs, salsa verde emulsion and citrus fruits makes a lasting impression… enjoyed in a delightful Alpine interior, tastefully decorated (old wood, light-coloured banquettes and seats, modern lighting), or on the terrace, with views of the mountains.

Name: De la Gare - La Table des Suter
Address: Avenue de la Gare 13, Lucens, 1522, Switzerland
Description: This family-run institution housed in a large ochre-coloured building in front of Lucens train station is a real hit. This is undoubtedly down to its winning combination of professionalism and a very warm welcome. The set menus include ambitious classic French dishes made from top-quality ingredients, eg "grand cru" beef cooked two ways, with a Pinot Noir sauce, Swiss chard and stuffed parmentine potatoes. The adjacent bistro also represents excellent value for money. And if you would like to extend your stay, there are neat and practical guestrooms available.

Name: Esprit Ravet
Description: The Ravet family from the L’Ermitage restaurant in Vufflens-le-Château have brought their own style to Hotel Bernerhof in the centre of Gstaad, in the form of this chic brasserie, which now serves ambitious modern French Ravet-style gourmet cuisine. The service is attentive and friendly. A special feature of the brasserie is a flambé trolley.

Name: Eat-Hola Tapas Bar
Description: Chef Sergi Arola designed and signed off on this menu, which includes his signature tapas – modern and creative small plates that are ideal for sharing. Tip: you can take a seat at the counter to watch the cooks at work and ask for their recommendations. The high tables are also a comfortable seating option. This trendy restaurant, the only tapas bar in this upscale resort, is located in the hotel W Verbier.

Name: Haberbüni
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: The atmosphere here is one of a kind! Housed in the airy hayloft of a 19C farmhouse with rustic beams, this place has a special feel to it. The tasteful interior is complemented by a secluded garden terrace with trees and shrubs. The food is fresh and made with high-quality ingredients. In the evening, there is a set menu and an à la carte selection. The latter is also available at lunchtime, supplemented by daily specials and a "Business Lunch" option. Excellent wine list featuring plenty of rarities and magnums.

Name: Ciani
Description: A fashionable restaurant housed in the Palazzo dei Congressi, where famous chef Dario Ranza delights guests with his fresh, Mediterranean cuisine. Don’t miss the delicious risottos, including his recipe with saffron, chanterelles, courgettes and Robiolino cheese. Excellent wine selection.

Name: Minamo
Description: With its pared-back Far Eastern decor and an eight-course traditional Japanese omakase menu served to all diners at the same time, this restaurant brings countertop dining and a slice of Japan to the exclusive Mandarin Oriental. From your comfortable seat at the counter, you can watch, for example, various nigiri being prepared before your very eyes – the chef will gladly expound on his work and philosophy. NB: There are a maximum of eight places available, so it is essential that you book!

Name: MOzern
Description: This part of the Mandarin Oriental's culinary portfolio serves food all day. In addition to lunch and dinner, you can have breakfast and afternoon tea here – all in tasteful surroundings that combine a stylish, old-world feel with a brasserie atmosphere. The menu includes Asian and classic dishes with options such as crispy duck rolls, "MOzern noodles", raclette cheese burgers and Angus beef tartare. The bar serves an excellent assortment of drinks and snacks. Tip: Drop in at the Grand Casino next door.

Name: LOFT FIVE
Description: This stylish restaurant stands directly on Europaallee, not far from the railway station (Hauptbahnhof). But it's not only the chic interior and relaxed atmosphere that are inviting – the food is also a definite draw! Flavoursome modern-inspired international cuisine is on the menu. The service is friendly and competent, and there is a good selection of wines and cocktails.

Name: Schloss Wartegg
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The elevated location between Lake Constance and the Alpstein is quite something! As in the small castle hotel, the focus in the restaurant, too, is on the organic and ecological. This translates into sustainably produced ingredients and organic produce from local suppliers, plus vegetables and herbs from the hotel's own 2 500m2garden. From the terrace there is a wonderful view of the countryside and Lake Constance.

Name: Le Restaurant / Le Relais
Description: If you are looking for excellence and elegance, you are in the right place at Le Restaurant or Le Relais of the venerable Badrutt's Palace! In an atmosphere of luxury, the attentive front-of-house team provides classic service. The flavourful cuisine is made from exclusive ingredients and the menu also features a number of dishes that are prepared at your table, e.g. flambées, tartar etc. Whatever you opt for, there is a first-class selection of wines from the best vineyards to accompany your meal. Tip: You can also have breakfast here - accompanied by views of the lake and mountains.

Name: S.Zimmer
Description: This cosy and intimate little restaurant is run by chef Stefan Zimmermann and hostess Tünde Tamàs. A most cordial family atmosphere awaits you, as well as flavoursome cuisine, with many of the ingredients being sourced from the region. They serve a set menu of up to seven courses. The wine list in particular shows influences from Hungary – the owner's homeland – and you should certainly consider her recommendations! Although located inside the building of Hotel Viktoria Eden, the restaurant is run independently.

Name: Jacques Restaurant
Description: Not far from the opera house is chef Jacques Allisson's "bistronomy" restaurant. His modern, creative and tasteful take on French cuisine is a hit, and the place is very popular. The atmosphere is relaxed, the service friendly and attentive. At lunchtime there is a business lunch; in the evening there are two set menus as well as à la carte dishes.

Name: FIVE
Description: Ensconced in the ski resort, with views of the Swiss mountains, elegant restaurant FIVE – part of the Guarda Golf Hotel – creates a contrast with its Levantine cuisine, which features mezze for sharing, among other dishes. Diners can also enjoy the European flavours of the desserts, including chocolate tart and fruit mousse.

Name: Birdy's by Achtien
Description: Perfect for anyone who loves to share! For lunch and dinner, chef Christian Vogel (aka Birdy) provides an exciting dining experience. With the "Sharing is Love" concept, he puts the onus on communication as much as culinary enjoyment in a relaxed, modern atmosphere. The cuisine is predominantly vegetarian, but can be supplemented with fish or meat – both of which are of the highest quality. Choose à la carte dishes such as cauliflower tempura, soy sauce, peanut, salted lemon, or roast Hokkaido pumpkin, peanut, Thai curry, kumquat, with optional fried Gotthard zander. The sharing surprise menu for two is also on point – ten dishes are served in three courses.

Name: Scaramouche
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Set in the affluent northern suburb of South Hill, Scaramouche has been a Toronto mainstay for decades, with Chef Keith Froggett at the helm since 1983. Don’t be alarmed when you arrive and head downstairs to the restaurant thinking you are off to a basement—you're not, as the superb city skyline view soon proves.Guests come for the views and stay for the traditional French cuisine. Don't expect modern twists, as dishes such as foie gras terrine with a sour cherry reduction and rabbit loin wrapped with bacon sided by a fricassee of sweet peas and fava beans, are as classic as they come. Savor the dark chocolate mousse with cherries for dessert, or take home one of their signature coconut cream pies.

Name: Actinolite
Description: This warm and welcoming restaurant on a residential stretch of Ossington Avenue takes its name from Chef Justin Cournoyer’s hometown, where he grew up hunting and foraging – an influence evident in his cooking. The unscripted, ever-evolving seven-course tasting menu is dictated by close relationships with local purveyors, who supply peak seasonal organic produce, wild-caught seafood and responsibly raised animals. The dishes, some of which are delivered and explained by the chefs themselves, display a sense of Nordic understatement; the homemade sourdough, served with yeast butter and accompanied by assorted meats, is always a highlight. In warmer months, the restaurant’s own garden supplies herbs and edible flowers.

Name: Jacobs & Co. Steakhouse
Description: Open since 2008, Jacobs & Co. feels like a local institution. It is the embodiment of a classic steakhouse, from its handsome looks—complete with a piano bar—to the emphasis on dry aging. Special touches abound; aged white cheddar popovers with roasted garlic and oregano butter arrive shortly after arrival, and they'll send you home with coffee cake muffins.Fresh oysters make for a nice opener, but if you're feeling flush, order the seafood tower. Then, tuck in to a 60-day dry aged rib eye. Thick and juicy, the steak imparts a slight nuttiness, while the variety of salts and sauces, including Japanese ponzu, chimichurri and whipped blue cheese with bacon, are a nice accompaniment. Desserts lean on tradition for a fitting end to a decadent meal.

Name: Ardo
Address: 243 King St. E., Toronto, M5A 1J9, Canada
Description: Inspiration comes from the sunny flavors of Southern Italy in this easygoing Old Town favorite, but the cooking isn’t overly preoccupied with tradition. For instance, nonna might not countenance the amount of butter that goes into a dish of orecchiette with sausage and rapini—but the indulgent results are unlikely to elicit any complaints. Scrupulously fresh seafood is a highlight, whether it be an albacore tuna carpaccio with celery and capers, or tender grilled octopus with marinated artichoke. It’s only fitting to end a meal with a spot-on rendition of cannoli with creamy ricotta filling. Those who are particularly smitten can take a bit of flavor home: the imported Sicilian olive oil, tomato sauce and pasta lining the walls are available for purchase.

Name: George
Address: 111C Queen St. E., Toronto, M5C 1S2, Canada
Description: Set in a red brick building that echoes the historic vibe of its surroundings, George has been one of Toronto's most popular restaurants since opening in 2003. Inside, the room exudes charm with its industrial bones mixed with an upscale bistro look and feel. A display kitchen turning out enjoyable cooking for the amiable crowd.Diners keep returning for always pleasing cuisine that features the likes of seared high-quality halibut nestled in potato puree dressed with finely diced, crispy lardons and sweet peas. In addition to à la carte, there is the choice of a 5-, 7- or 10-course tasting which the chef composes spontaneously.Half-pour cocktails and 3- or 5-oz glasses of wine are just right for those who prefer to imbibe with restraint.

Name: Amal
Address: 131 Bloor St. W., Toronto, M5S 1R1, Canada
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Brunch,Credit cards not accepted,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Looking for a bite to eat in between shopping and sightseeing? Amal, with a sexy, sleek, mod Middle Eastern look and ambient vibe, is just the place. Tables are always in demand here, but the smartly dressed service team handles it all seamlessly. Weekends are especially buzzy thanks to a DJ spinning tunes.Expect modern presentations of classic Lebanese and Middle Eastern dishes prepared with authenticity, heart and refinement. Order a few mezze to start—perhaps the seared halloumi or truffle rakakat, a plate of crisp pastry rolls dipped in pistachios and filled with truffle-infused cream. Then, a delicious skewer or char-grilled chicken Tawok are worthy orders. Baklava, that classic dessert, is always a good idea.

Name: Vela
Description: With exposed brick, a bar that goes on and on, and lights swirled into a sloped ceiling, this cool-kids restaurant has wide appeal. There is certainly seating for all occasions: white banquettes in the back, an up-close chef’s counter and plenty of tables in between. By design, the menu has faint Asian touches but is otherwise broad in its selection of seafood, pastas, steaks and vegetables. The results? Surprisingly dialed-in, largely thanks to a kitchen that makes as much as it can in-house. Highlights include cod with beurre blanc and chili crisp and, for dessert, a sugar-crusted profiterole filled with miso dulce de leche mousse and mascarpone cremeaux. Live music throughout the week will either attract or deter, depending on your mood.

Name: Koh Lipe Thai Kitchen
Description: Koh Lipe stands out among its Chinatown neighbors for its lively atmosphere and its authentic southern Thai cooking. Set over two floors and boasting a popular terrace, this place just feels fun, a mood buoyed by the friendly young staff.The kitchen dishes out regional specialties that deliver heat and flavor in spades. Coconut green curry beef with plantain and stink bean is a classic bowl of piping hot, delicious comfort. The chef's specials are always a sure bet, but for those diners who may be less familiar with Thai food, the noodle dishes are a perfect introduction. Don’t worry if there is a line—they turn around tables swiftly, so you won’t be waiting long to bite into those meaty prawn tails served with a kicky lime-chili dip.

Name: Musoshin Ramen
Description: Hiding just off the main drag in Roncesvalles, this restaurant is not like other ramen-yas. For starters, none of them can bake like Chef Aoi Yoshida, who turns out trays of perfectly formed Japanese milk bread and other sweet treats. Her house-made noodles, bundled into every bowl, are also a cut above most. But perhaps the most fascinating part of this restaurant hides in the broths. Whereas a typical tonkotsu ramen favors heart-stopping, porky richness, the style here is a vegetable base that is both lighter and leaner and yet equally savory. In a testament to both her own talents and to modern technology, Yoshida learned both noodle and ramen craft by video chatting with an old friend who runs this restaurant’s original location in Kyoto.

Name: Dil Se
Description: Dil Se is set along the village's main thoroughfare in Toronto's "Roncy" neighborhood. Effort has gone into the decor here, with linen-draped tables and walls accented by colorful fabrics.Chef/owner Mani Panwar offers highly enjoyable, well-prepared northern Indian cuisine.Paneer lababdar, a "Chef's special," is a Mughlai-style specialty featuring soft cubes of fresh cow's milk cheese simmered in a creamy, highly flavorful, orange-hued sauce enriched with cashews. Neatly presented in a metal bowl, vegetable biryani is fluffy and hot with a bright flavor courtesy of chilies, herbs and dried spices. Among the tandoor offerings, choose the lamb seek kebab, which comes with a zesty red chutney that leans tart.

Name: Maha's
Description: Homesick for Egypt, Maha Barsoom opened her eponymous restaurant in 2014, and it's been a good thing for Leslieville residents ever since. Climb the steps to land in the coffee bar, then immediately order the epic honey-cardamom latte.This homey spot serves breakfast and lunch only. Lentil soup is an absolute must. Local lore says it's what sparked her to open Maha's, and after one spoonful you'll see why. The warm bowl delivers sharp tartness courtesy of vinegar-soaked Vidalia onions; charred mini pita adds a creamy body and garlic tomatoes share a sweet acidity. The Cairo classic is another go-to. This tender fava bean stew is plated with a fluffy orb of falafel and slices of hard boiled egg, then sided by an impossibly soft balady.

Name: Aloette
Description: Open since 2017, this stylish bistro remains one of the coolest reservations in town. Chef Patrick Kriss and his well-oiled restaurant group again demonstrate that they have the Midas touch. With the tasting menu-only ALO just upstairs, the team here is impressively polished in this diner setting. No wider than a train car, the cozy space offers satisfying, approachable dishes that look and taste far better than imagined. Iceberg wedges dressed in chive cream arrive under a mountain of puffed wild rice. A complimentary loaf of cheddar brioche wouldn’t be out of place on white tablecloth. Everyone wants the burger. And for dessert, there must be pie. The signature lemon meringue is a towering finale that will have you rolling out the door.

Name: Ten
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Wheelchair access
Description: Named after both the number of seats at the counter and the courses served, Ten is an original concept offering unapologetically vegetable-focused cuisine. Beyond a serving of kampachi, scallops from Nova Scotia or duck sourced from a local farm, this small kitchen run by the young Chef Julian Bentivegna cooks only what the season provides and does so with notable creativity. Some dishes on the tasting menu lean new Nordic minimalist; others, like a butterball potato pavé paired with nutty salsa matcha, tangy fermented radish and earthy sweet black garlic, zigzag across culinary borders. A recent highlight featured a silky-smooth mix of beets and lime juice set in a buttery almond tart. The minimalist, all-white space keeps all eyes on the food.

Name: Alder
Description: The stylish Ace hotel scored big when the industrious Chef Patrick Kriss moved into the ground level. The restaurant is a cool mix of dark brick floors, sleek wood finishes and large windows that usher in radiant beams of sunlight. And true to everything that the Alo Food Group does, expect a serious kitchen brigade and equally serious cooking. There’s a lot to like on this Mediterranean menu. Beef carpaccio is a crowd-pleaser, while the cucumber salad is a sleeper hit festooned with shaved fennel, dukkah, and hazelnuts. Stacks of firewood in the dining room is a clue to hone-in on proteins like roast chicken, Australian lamb, and a bone-in strip loin. Dessert is a must, especially if the astoundingly light coconut cream pie is still around.

Name: Bar Chica
Description: Bar or not? It's debatable, but what's safe to say is Bar Chica is bursting with vitality in every way. This is a cool place for cool people and it's quietly making its mark on the city. Foodies in the know  come for their unique take on tapas and a sherry or two. The servers' beaming smiles light the place up, and that passion follows through to the kitchen where they put their all into every plate. Expect a colorful plate of heirloom tomatoes & ajo blanco in the ensalada and fluffy grated truffle on their version of croqueta de jamon. Save room for the delectable torta de chocolate.Chica is easy to miss with its minimal exterior so keep a look out for the glowing lantern above the door, then settle in for a great night out.

Name: Henry's
Address: 922 Queen St. W., Toronto, M6J 1G6, Canada
Description: Of the city’s many, many wine bars, Henry’s is both the newest and one of the most accomplished. Globe lighting, forest green cushions and gold-trim tables lend a certain mid-century modern sleekness to this inviting, airy space, which includes a backyard patio and a retail wine shop just next door.The menu makes no commitments to any one cuisine, beyond working exceptionally well with the wines on hand. You could assemble dinner solely out of appetizers like beef tartare with smoked crème fraiche, shrimp toast and fried zucchini blossoms. But then you’d miss that superb skate wing set in a fiery curry. Some might choose wine for their dessert, but a recent ancho-chili and chocolate mousse made a compelling case for never skipping sweets here.

Name: Adrak Yorkville
Description: How many dining rooms could you describe as regal? This is surely one of them. No expense was spared in the design, with hand-carved furniture, cushy, turmeric-colored booths lining the walls and striking archways all basking in a golden aura. But good looks can only take you so far, and this kitchen rises to the occasion with precisely seasoned, carefully cooked dishes inspired from regions all across India. A fiery thecha paneer tikka showcases creativity while crisp garlic naan and meaty kebabs roasted in clay tandoor ovens are a nod to familiar favorites. One very fragrant chicken biryani baked under puff pastry and served with a sauce of peanuts, chilies and yogurt stands as a refreshing change of pace from the standard preparation.

Name: Parquet
Description: French bistros can be predictable, but this neighborhood corner in Harbord Village takes a wonderfully refreshing approach. One could spend all day taking in the design: The marble bar is a worthy perch for admiring the gorgeous, patterned floors, forest-green ceiling and stylish, wood-paneled walls. And that patio – it’s a summer oasis. The cooking, meanwhile, hits all the right marks, and feels unquestionably French in its richness and satisfaction. Who knew that mushroom beignets could be so light and pair so well with lime and pepper sauce? One could make a meal out of the roasted cauliflower with cumin vinaigrette and puffed chickpeas. Cassoulet with duck confit and steak frites with béarnaise are proper classics.

Name: Union
Description: Butchers, artisan bakers, antique shops and coffee shops define this stretch of Ossington Avenue where the appealingly worn Union awaits. There is a horseshoe-shaped bar at the entrance, but head back to the rustic brick-faced dining room. If you're up for a bit of theater, nab a seat at the counter to catch the action.Chef/owner Teo Paul once worked on a farm and his menu is a love letter to the region's seasons and its local suppliers. Lunch is perfect for a quick bite, while dinner is more of an event. Dishes are rustic with a refined edge and pack a flavorful punch.. The same effort and care goes into an omelette as steak frites, and if servers are busy, expect the chef himself to serve your plate, along with an explanation of what's on it.

Name: Lapinou
Address: 642 King St. W., Toronto, M5V 1M7, Canada
Description: Chilly Toronto nights call for cozy spaces, and Lapinou delivers in spades with its beamed ceiling, vintage-style oil lamps, forest green booths and an eye-catching green-veined marble bar. Just west of the Theater District in an area teeming with standout spots, Lapinou pulls its weight with a fresh spin on classic bistro fare. Don't confuse tried and true with ho-hum though, as Chef Jamie Ullrich carefully balances tradition with intrigue. Shrimp cocktail is a simple but elegant starter, as is the perfect disc of beef tartare topped with an egg yolk and sided by sourdough toast. Duck confit is comfort in a casserole dish with buttery white flageolet beans and garlicky andouille sausage. The delightful tarte au cafe rounds out the enjoyable experience.

Name: Buca
Address: 604 King St. W., Toronto, M5V 1M6, Canada
Description: Note: Temporarily closed Tucked underground through an alleyway entrance, this hideout is nonetheless a very poorly kept secret, drawing acclaim from all quarters with its hearty, meat-centric Italian fare. For starters, a notable selection of salumi is artfully cured and aged in house, showcasing carefully sourced heritage breed pork in exemplary versions of coppa or prosciuttini (sliced wafer-thin, naturally). Handmade pastas and crisp Roman-style pizzas both vie for attention, with intriguing accoutrements like wild boar soppressata and Calabrese-style braised pork—a dilemma best resolved by covering more ground with a group. Note that a second location on Scollard shifts focus to the fruits of the ocean, as in buttery Nova Scotia lobster matched with fresh angel hair pasta.

Name: La Banane
Description: It may have something to do with the crowd of artists, movie stars and sophisticates who have made this their perch. Or, it could be the ambience defined by rich, seductive colors and loud, high-energy music. Either way, it's all very hip and very cool at La Banane. The cooking is equally lavish, featuring a well-stocked raw bar, wagyu steaks and plenty of truffle and foie gras in between. Start your evening at the elegant bar with a perfectly chilled shrimp cocktail before digging into Salt Spring mussels with Normandy cider and crème fraiche. Beef flatiron set in a delicious sauce au poivre is a classic done right. And to finish, don’t miss the Gâteau à la banane, a sweet cake accompanied by salted caramel ice cream and caramelized bananas.

Name: Bar Isabel
Description: Right on bustling College Street, Bar Isabel charms diners with its old-world tavern vibe and broad appeal. Perfect for groups, it's also just right for solo diners, as some some dishes may be prepared in half portions, inviting exploration. Chef Grant van Gameren's cooking is heartfelt and there is never anything frilly or overwrought on his Spanish tapas menu. Dishes are rustic and straightforward and there is a clear focus on quality flavors married with strong product. Case in point? The pork secreto, which takes a flavorful grilled pork cheek and ratchets it up a notch with a honey and apple cider reduction. The craft beer list is interesting, and there are plenty of ciders, Spanish wine and cocktails, particularly those employing Sherry, on offer.

Name: Canoe
Description: In 2025 this iconic restaurant will celebrate its 30th anniversary. The views from its position on the 54th floor of the TD Bank Tower are unmatched in the city and service is as efficient as you’d expect from such a well-oiled machine. Lunchtime is largely the reserve of Bay Street brokers and bankers; the menu is an easily navigable document for those whose business is business and who don’t want to hang around too long. At dinner, the pace slows and the menu expands to reveal the full extent of the kitchen’s capabilities. Wild Pacific halibut is paired with Savoy cabbage and champagne cream; while lamb saddle is accompanied by its braised shoulder. For dessert, look no further than the tarte au sucre.

Name: Mimi Chinese
Description: Lipstick red banquettes and servers fitted in sharp suits make for a different kind of Chinese restaurant. Unlike the homestyle comforts and flavors of its sibling Sunnys, this Yorkville looker pulls in an equally gussied-up crowd out for an upscale evening. The kitchen takes regional classics and spins them with just enough style. The shrimp toast, brilliantly made with fried bread and a hot mustard mayo, is worth a visit alone, but don't miss out on the scallop crudo with fried donut and that soulful soy broth. Spice-hounds will be all over the Hunan chili sea bass, and someone should probably order the picturesque “four-foot belt noodle.” There’s plenty to drink too, with sharp cocktails and a thorough selection of baijiu.

Name: Gia
Address: 1214 Dundas St. W., Toronto, M6J1X5, Canada
Description: Panko-crusted meatballs, crab cakes with bagna cauda, pappardelle Bolognese. You could have a full dinner at this narrow hotspot in Trinity Bellwoods and not even realize that everything is meatless. Such is the charm of Jenny Coburn’s latest, plant-forward restaurant, which replaces her previous spot, Ufficio. High ceilings, exposed white brick, herringbone floors and a constantly packed dining room make for a stylish night out. House-made pasta is the prime order here, with one dish that has carried over from the previous restaurant: porcini agnolotti glossed in a sauce of butter and Parmigiano Reggiano, which can be made with vegan butter upon request. Unable to land a reservation? Walk-ins can snag a seat at the cozy, walnut-topped bar.

Name: Madrina Bar y Tapas
Description: Located in the center of the historic Distillery District in a space that seamlessly blends old and new, this lively spot impresses with its style and swagger. Madrina translates to godmother, though their interpretation has a whimsical bent.Chef Ramon Simarro pens a tribute to his native Catalan region with a lengthy tapas menu balancing classic and modern bites for a dynamic experience. Classics like pan con tomate hold their own, while the creative, modern twists are bold, yet grounded by solid techniques and quality ingredients. Sweet tapas, such as rice pudding croquetas, round out the meal.From a Spanish-focused wine list to an interesting cocktail menu with a designated gin and tonic section, the sips are equally compelling.

Name: Bar Vendetta
Address: 928 Dundas St. W., Toronto, M6J 1W3, Canada
Description: Anyone with a kitchen no bigger than a hotel closet should look to this narrow nook for inspiration. Truly, it is a wonder how restaurateur Jen Agg and her team manage to turn out so many from-scratch breads and pastas. Rosemary focaccia, tagliatelle alfredo and pappardelle twirled around oxtail ragu are just some of the hearty offerings at this favored wine bar in Dundas West. The signature dish is a cacio e pepe-inspired coil of ricotta-stuffed pasta. White-and-orange tile flooring, vintage posters and wood tones, along with welcoming servers, create a come-as-you-are, retro vibe. Some guests aren’t even here to eat. Instead, they’ve come to sidle up to the long bar and dig into the surprisingly lengthy, Italian-leaning wine list.

Name: Giulietta
Description: Every neighborhood deserves a reliable hotspot that cooks, pours and serves with remarkable ease. Dufferin Grove has this in Giulietta, a stylish (but not too stylish) Italian looker by Chef Rob Rossi. Even if you don’t live nearby, this talented team treats every guest like a long-time VIP. And the food? This is cooking that comforts, thanks to a kitchen that makes the most out of every dish on the menu. Yellowfin tuna crudo with bergamot marmalade is a vibrant way to begin before moving into heartier dishes. A diner might attempt ordering both the ricotta agnolotti with morels as well as the mafalde with veal cheek ragu, but don't forget pizza. Charred, puffy and dressed with smart ingredients, the savory pie is greedily delicious.

Name: Chubby's Jamaican Kitchen
Description: The warm breezes of the Caribbean might be far away, but even in the dead of winter, stepping into this lively haven will bring a bit of island sunshine. Warm, easygoing hospitality is matched by homey, unpretentious cooking, with traditional dishes whose humble appearances belie surprising depth of flavor. "Likkle bites" like saltfish fritters are a fine starter, but don't let them distract you from exemplary versions of comforting classics like curry goat or oxtail stew (and take urgent note that the gravy from either can be ordered as a side). Perhaps best of all is the succulent jerk chicken, expertly cooked over a wood-burning grill to achieve an ethereal marriage of smoke, sweetness and spice—as good as any you’re likely to find this far from a beach.

Name: Prime Seafood Palace
Address: 944 Queen St. W., Toronto, M6J 1G8, Canada
Description: To find the front door, you’ll have to follow your nose. The scent of barbecue wafts down an alleyway fitted with stacks of firewood. Inside, find a dazzling space lined with maple slats, a domed ceiling and salmon-pink booths and walls. There is nothing like it around, and no surprise that Chef Matty Matheson is the mastermind here behind the city’s newest and most ambitious steakhouse. The menu is tightly curated balancing fantastic seafood, big meats cooked on the grill and serious vegetable preparations. Sicilian crudo and delicate ricotta dumplings are proper preludes to a bone-in dry-aged strip loin. Supplements like palace potatoes, cacio e pepe-inspired cauliflower and steamed carrots with pink shrimp aim to be more than sideshows.

Name: The Wood Owl
Description: This quaint, wooden shoebox is a welcome retreat in Danforth. Wine bottles line the perimeter of a room that has a pleasant sepia tint. In fact, there’s no pretense at all here, which in part is what makes this restaurant so appealing. The menu is small, nothing extravagant or overly complicated, and offers far more vegetables than one might expect from a wine bar (adobo- roasted carrots with green goddess, anyone?). Beef, though, is still very much welcome at the table, highlighted as a weekly special, usually paired with a superb tangle of shoestring French fries. With or without a reservation, you should take a seat, order the fried polenta cakes with romesco and boquerones, and relish in the ease of a place that gets all the little details right.

Name: Antler
Address: 1454 Dundas St. W., Toronto, M6J 1Y6, Canada
Description: This small chef-run restaurant in quaint Little Portugal is cozy and rustic with a welcoming bar, walls of exposed brick and forest scenes and, yes, a mounted deer with antlers (naturally). Chef/co-owner Michael Hunter lives and breathes by the locally sourced and grown ethos, and takes it up a notch by focusing on game. First up, a carrot and smoked ricotta salad. Sound boring? It's anything but, with roasted heirloom carrots and ribbons of yellow and red raw carrots over a pool of creamy, smoked ricotta. Then, pan-seared and roasted Ontario venison, bathed in a green peppercorn sauce and served with a wedge of hot Boulangère potatoes, hits all the right notes. For dessert, pear tart Tatin is a wedge of pure bliss.

Name: Kiin
Address: 326 Adelaide St. W., Toronto, M5V 1R3, Canada
Description: Chef Nuit Regular impresses with her elaborate, one-of-a-kind vision of royal Thai cuisine. The elegant space is a prime setting for equally elegant dishes, which are presented with flair. Colorful mounds of rice, pineapple and dumplings shaped like flowers, and so much more arrive in petite forms in small bowls and on large platters. The dishes themselves will ring familiar, from Isan-style sausage and larb, to hot and sour beef soup and the famed khao soi, all of it seasoned and spiced in a measured manner. The tender Boombai short rib glossed in a dark curry is a particular standout. First-timers should start with the signature chef’s tasting, which nearly covers the entire menu alongside a few bonus dishes.

Name: Mother's Dumplings
Description: Chef-owner Zhen Feng has folded so many dumplings for Toronto that she might as well be the city’s honorary mother. In 2005 she opened a small, eight-table nook on Huron Street. Five years later, she relocated to a much larger space and by then had boiled, steamed and pan-fried her way to becoming a city institution in the heart of Chinatown. The menu boasts all manner of Chinese dishes, but stick to the namesake specialty, which are rolled out and folded at all hours by a dedicated team in the back. One could make a meal out of just the boiled pork and dill dumplings, but other types are also worth dipping into. On the way out, bags of frozen dumplings are available for take-home when the craving hits and Feng’s kitchen is closed for the day.

Name: PAI
Description: Named for the Thai village where Nuit Regular and her husband opened their first restaurant, PAI is perpetually busy. A former nurse, Nuit now soothes by cooking her family recipes and street food favorites for hungry patrons. The mod bohemian look is appealing, but it's the extensive menu that you'll spend all of your time admiring. It's full of fresh, tasty dishes and vibrant curries. While they traipse across Thailand for inspiration, zero in on the North Thai plates and chef favorites, including khao soi, a noodle and coconut milk dish, or kanom jin nham ngeaw, a pork rib and tomato soup with rice vermicelli. Kung tawt, a plate of fried shrimp sided by a piquant tamarind sauce, is delicious but gaeng panang, a sweet-and-sour red curry, hits all the right notes.

Name: SARA
Description: Sara, with its cool, almost monastic modernity, is a place to keep the outside world at bay—the tables are even designed with center compartments for storing phones. Reconnection and shared experiences seem to be the theme here, where a globally inspired, contemporary shared plates menu takes center stage. Fret not if you've arrived solo, as many dishes are available in half-portions for a deeper survey of the kitchen's ability. And able they are. Standouts include ikura latkes, featuring two butternut squash latkes topped with a lemon chive crème fraîche, smoked ikura and finished with a maple kombu drizzle. Alaskan king crab is served with a nuoc cham sauce and topped with crispy fried rice finished with avocado, curls of scallion and cilantro.

Name: CÀ PHÊ RANG
Description: This collaboration between Chef Matty Matherson and his mentor Rang Nguyen has established itself as a firm favorite on Spadina for lovers of Vietnamese food. One bite of the banh mi with succulent roasted pork and you’ll be transported back to Ho Chi Minh City on that backpacker’s trip you once took. The bowls of pho will warm the bones and gladden the heart – the sliced rare beef is well worth ordering – and the chicken wings are cooked to order in a kitchen that appears to be almost the same size as the dining area. The prices are fair, the service helpful and efficient and the room has a colorful, bright, laid-back vibe. For a quick refuel or a bite with friends, this little place might just hit the spot.

Name: Viaggio
Address: 1727 Dundas St. W., Toronto, M6K 1V4, Canada
Description: You might consider dropping by even if it means you can only order dessert. A novel effort that feels part soufflé, part pancake, the signature tiramisu finished with espresso maple syrup and whipped mascarpone may very well be one of the best desserts in the city. Many dishes, in fact, feel unique to this neighborhood charmer, which could have very easily played it safe with standard Italian dishes. However, this is a kitchen that chooses to top pizzas with smoked pastrami and sauerkraut and chooses to toss tagliolini with charred octopus glossed in smoked dashi butter. Refreshingly creative, such moves pay off in delicious ways.The historic building boasts a handsome dining room as well as an inviting deck lit with strung garden lights.

Name: 156 Cumberland
Description: Pockets of fried tofu skin stuffed with gochujang beef tartare topped with fried onions. Hand-torn noodles with seared baby scallops, zucchini puree and parmesan. On a packed street squished among a jigsaw puzzle of stores, this quirky Yorkville restaurant doesn’t fit neatly in a box, but that’s the point. A young team has designed a small menu grounded in Korean cooking with global inspiration. Guests looking for something a little more familiar but nonetheless refined should swing for the beef short ribs, marinated in a sweet kalbi soy and paired with grilled maitake and spinach namool. The space is minimally designed with strawberry-pink walls and white kitchen tile on the ground floor and a darker, more business-friendly setting upstairs.

Name: Dreyfus
Description: No obvious signage, curtains drawn and the front door frosted top to bottom. What could this cozy French bistro be hiding? The answer is indulgence. Situated on the first floor of a narrow townhouse, Dreyfus is the kind of dinner you have before hibernation and after an annual physical. Rare (and sadly empty) trophy wines line the room’s perimeter, while servers explain that the fries are for the pâté and that the doughnuts are for the smoked trout dip garnished with roe. That Zach Kolomeir cooks with maximum impact shouldn’t be a shock given his tenure at Montreal’s famed Joe Beef. Sitting elbow to elbow, oenophiles looking for primo vino will have to ask for off-menu bottles, some of which sit in plain sight above the bar.

Name: Pho Tien Thanh
Description: This spot set off busy Queen Street may not bother with frills or fuss but this place fills early with patrons willing to wait in line. They're here for the food—classic Vietnamese dishes including pho and other specialties—that is delivered from stove to tabletop in no time. Attractive presentations and a clear attention to detail with quality ingredients make the experience all the more pleasing. Hearty bowls of Pho are the way to go; the rare beef variations are especially impressive. Big steaming bowls may be the signature, but the menu does offer many other dishes that are worth exploring.While you'll hopefully arrive with an empty stomach, come with a full wallet, since it's cash or debit card only (though there is an on-site ATM).

Name: Aanch
Address: 259 Wellington St. W., Toronto, M5V 3P9, Canada
Description: Some things never change, like the stylish, tranquil setting of this restaurant, which opened under a different name (and chef) over a decade ago. The menu is lengthy and covers a wide swath of familiar, regional dishes, from the famous deep-fried chicken 65 of Chennai to the sharp, fiery vindaloos of Goa. Efforts to gussy up the plating with swirls and dots of sauce can come across as superfluous, but the end result is still a delicious one. Fried cones of paneer dusted in mango powder showcase the kitchen’s modern sensibilities, while the butter-rich dal bukhari seasoned with garam masala is a trusted classic. Heat levels across the board are on the mild side so chili hounds will have to request for extra kick, if so inclined.

Name: FK
Address: 770 St. Clair Ave. W., Toronto, M6C 1B5, Canada
Description: In a sun-drenched space that could pass for a precious tearoom, this neighborhood gem is a reliable crowd-pleaser. Colorful, market-driven cooking starts with excellent, crusty house bread made with garlic scapes, sundried tomatoes, olives or whatever else the chef has in mind. Are soft shell crabs in season? Is it time for morels? Such questions are front of mind for this honest kitchen, which doesn’t get too fussy with the cooking. Familiar flavors ring true in hearty entrees like the meltingly tender Cornish hen brushed in a smoky-sweet barbecue sauce. Fresh pasta, like the braised oxtail tortellini, conveniently comes in appetizer portions. The pacing here can be a bit leisurely, but when the food is this satisfying, what’s the hurry?

Name: Bistro Pinot
Description: Are you in Friesland and dreaming of a getaway to Paris? Then make your way through the lovely streets of Grou to this delightful bistro. The nostalgic wall tiles, the marble counter and wooden stools, the French music pouring out of the speakers… This place has real character! Bistro classics are prepared in time-honoured tradition here: succulent foie gras on brioche, zesty canard à l'orange, a crispy and wonderfully fresh macaroon tart. The dishes for sharing (choose at least four) transport you to those iconic bistros of the Parisian Left Bank.

Name: Nazka
Description: You might, for a moment, feel as if you have stumbled across a wine cellar, but you will soon see that this hip South American eatery is very much at home in this cosmopolitan city. Nazka unleashes a whirlwind of bold flavours on your palate, from pisco cocktails to ceviche and other Peruvian specialities. This is exhilarating cuisine featuring a captivating interplay of spicy and sweet chilli peppers, Asian umami and the zing of leche del tigre. The well-curated selection of wines from around the globe adds extra character to this unique dining experience.

Name: Fricska 2.0
Description: Fricska has been reborn, only this time with a slight speakeasy vibe. Its unassuming exterior gives nothing away, but downstairs you’ll find a bright and trendy bar-cum-restaurant with a modern bistro feel. The food is a perfect match, with traditional dishes lightened and modernised to take on an appealingly fresh style. The lunch menu is a steal and the chocolate soufflé is a sure-fire hit. Service is smooth and attentive, and the friendly team will happily guide you through the fully Hungarian wine list.

Name: Végállomás Bistro&Wine
Description: It might be tucked away in the suburbs, but this neighbourhood bistro is so highly regarded that plenty of people come from further afield. The cosy terrace has its own wooden bar, and the split-level interior has a relaxed, traditional feel. The ever-evolving menu of seasonal dishes offers something for everyone, and the lunchtime options are great value; keep an eye out for the Bird’s milk and orange egg white foam dessert.

Name: Spago by Wolfgang Puck
Description: Austrian chef Wolfgang Puck has brought his fun Californian dining concept to Budapest. Set within the Matild Palace Hotel, close to the Elisabeth Bridge, it comes with a large terrace, and is a hot ticket in town. Appealing, unfussy dishes are well-executed – go for one of the pastas.

Name: Víg Molnár Csárda
Description: This traditional looking tavern comes with plenty of character and is certainly a hit with the locals. There’s a rustic, slightly Mediterranean feel to the décor, but the best place to sit is on the large terrace beside the working water wheel. Fairly priced, hearty Hungarian classics are the order of the day, and you’ll be well looked after by the friendly owners and their team.

Name: Sauska 48
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: Find a table on the spacious terrace to enjoy wonderful views out across the vineyard of this modern winery. Contemporary Hungarian dishes feature on a concise menu; this is rustic cooking with a refined edge and clear, bold flavours. The wines come from the vines you see in front of you, as well as from the owners’ other winery in Tokaj. The friendly service team cope well with the numbers.

Name: Natura Hill
Description: The climb up the steep, narrow lane is worth it, as the Danube Bend views from the two-hectare estate are breathtaking. True to its name, this restaurant follows a natural, ‘slow food’ ethos; locally sourced ingredients underpin the cooking and dishes are fresh, unfussy and vibrantly flavoured. The menus are decided upon twice a day as new produce arrives – come for the ‘Spontaneous Bistro Lunch’ or the tasting menu at dinner. This is a holistic place in which to stay, complete with a sauna, wellness centre and bedrooms; ask for a first floor room with a balcony.

Name: Platán Bisztró
Description: Set within the same historic building as Platán Gourmet is this lovely bistro with a relaxed, contemporary style. In summer, the setting is idyllic: you can dine beneath the branches of a more than 230-year-old tree on a lovely, stepped terrace bordering a lake. The concise menu sees Hungarian dishes given a refined bistro-style makeover, and service is warm and chatty. A hotel and spa are also part of the Platán complex.

Name: Csopaki Resti by Laurel
Description: The old village railway station plays host to this tiny 10-seater restaurant, where the raised seats at the counter are the best place to sit. Little sister to Laurel in Budapest, its multi-course set menu follows the same ethos, with modern dishes keeping Hungarian flavours to the fore. Watch the chefs preparing the dishes – before serving them personally – or, in summer, head out to the terrace, where they serve street food cooked on the Big Green Egg.

Name: 84 Bisztró
Description: The rather elegant Hazai Provence wellness hotel plays host to this rustic-chic bistro with a covered terrace. It’s personally run by a hands-on couple: she cooks, while he looks after their guests. They used to live in Spain and loved travelling to Italy, so you’ll find both Mediterranean and Hungarian influences in the cooking, with homemade pasta a speciality. The main menu is concise but supplemented by a blackboard of seasonal specials.

Name: Solid
Description: The rooftop of the Rum Hotel plays host to the sister of Salt, which opens for dinner from Tuesday to Saturday and offers great views over the river. In winter, it’s covered and there’s a warming fireplace; in summer, the roof is retracted and the sun streams in. They style themselves as a wine bar and the global list focuses on natural and biodynamic options. The menu, meanwhile, comprises classic Hungarian dishes reworked in a modern style and presented as a selection of small and large sharing plates.

Name: füge
Address: Tihany Yacht Club, Rév utca 7, Tihany, 8237, Hungary
Description: If you’re visiting in season, make for this bright lakeside restaurant with a chilled vibe. Many of the yachts in the nearby private mooring belong to regular guests, who have crossed Lake Balaton to enjoy either modern Asian-inspired dishes, or pizzas fresh from the oven located on the attractive terrace. Attentive service and bedrooms – some with balconies and water views – make this a great all-round package.

Name: Umo
Description: There are two parts to this restaurant found within a boutique hotel: a contemporary brasserie in the atrium, and an enclosed courtyard to the back of the building. The latter was formerly a monastery and is a wonderful place to sit – it comes complete with an open kitchen where dishes are cooked over flames and smoke. Alongside modernised Hungarian classics you’ll find a great butchery section, as well as the occasional South American or Asian influence.

Name: Zelna Borbisztró
Description: A smart, modern wine bar in the livelier part of this seasonal town, Zelna is named after the wine company whose wines it serves – and also offers for purchase. This is a place to kick back and relax, and the small menu mixes lighter and more substantial Hungarian dishes so you can tailor-make your own experience – just be sure to save room for the golden walnut dumplings! Every table is located on the large terrace, which stays open until 2am.

Name: 67 Sigma
Description: Start with a stroll around the pretty Old Town, then head to this historic property tucked away on a cobbled street; you enter via an enclosed courtyard and terrace, into a smart restaurant with plenty of atmosphere. Good quality produce is used to create fresh, flavoursome Hungarian dishes in a modern style. Courteous service comes from a local team.

Name: Piac 42
Description: The more casual sister to Michelin-Starred 42 is a smart, informal bistro set amongst upmarket artisan businesses in the recently opened Esztergom Market. Find a seat in the cosy bistro-cum-bar or on the sun-drenched terrace and choose from a concise menu of fresh, flavour-packed dishes crafted from local produce. Tradition leads the way, with the likes of pork rillettes and pancakes with cottage cheese. Come for breakfast, a leisurely lunch or a lively evening out.

Name: Kővirág
Description: The village of Köveskál is starting to gain something of a reputation for its gastronomy. This charming farmhouse sits at its centre and comes with a vintage-chic style and a pretty candlelit terrace. Service is incredibly welcoming, and the unfussy, well-delivered dishes come with a Hungarian heart and modern overtones. Wines are carefully sourced from the local area.

Name: Rókusfalvy Fogadó
Description: This pretty roadside inn is proudly owned and run by a local winemaker and comes with plenty of olde worlde charm. As you’d hope, the menu is a carefully prepared selection of classic Hungarian dishes, and the wines are from their own vineyard and other nearby wineries. The inviting terrace is a great place to sit when the weather’s right, and there are restful bedrooms should you wish to stay the night.

Name: Villa Kabala
Description: Perched high up the hillside in the Badacsony region, with far reaching views of Lake Balaton, this period villa was once home to artist István Farkas. Now under the ownership of an ambitious and enthusiastic couple, the team here are establishing it as something of a destination restaurant. Go for the well-balanced tasting menu and paired wines – you won’t get much more local than this, with the cheese, salami, sausages, beers and wines all family made. Book a bedroom with a terrace and look forward to a fantastic breakfast.

Name: IKON
Description: Set on a main street in the heart of the city, IKON stands out among the other eateries for its smart look, structured service and confident cooking. The chef spent time working in England and his dishes are an intriguing mix of reworked Hungarian classics and some British influences – go for something from the ‘Traditions Reborn’ section and be sure not to miss dessert. For a more immersive experience, book the chic Kitchen Table.

Name: Stand25 Bisztró
Description: There’s always a contented buzz to this neighbourhood bistro on the Buda side of the Danube. It’s owned by the same team as Stand, so their ethos around quality is the same, and you’ll be looked after by a slick team. Cooking focuses on Hungarian classics with a Mediterranean edge and, while dishes are hearty with robust flavours, they also have a refined edge.

Name: Textúra
Description: Set almost opposite its sister restaurant, Borkonyha Winekitchen, is this stylish, design-led brasserie with a relaxed atmosphere, a living wall of moss and a central wooden ‘tree’. Seasonally led dishes are ambitious and creative, and there are some real gems from Hungary on the wine list.

Name: FELIX Kitchen & Bar
Description: Felix sits behind the breathtaking neo-renaissance façade of the former Várkert Kiosk, in a building which once pumped water to the Royal Palace. It’s a plush place, with a stunningly restored ceiling and an air-conditioned terrace. The luxurious menu sees caviar sitting alongside signature dishes and grills.

Name: Onyx Mühely
Description: The rebirth of Onyx is underway… starting with Onxy Mühely, a 16-seater test kitchen which offers dishes that will go on to form the core of the menu at the new Onyx (set to open in 2024). All guests arrive at the same time for drinks and nibbles, before being shown through to an elegant ‘workshop’ with a beautiful open kitchen and a glass-enclosed, galleried library. Diners are also invited to be critics and are encouraged to talk to the chefs and leave written feedback on the menu. Sustainability is a focus of the refined dishes, and the whole experience is interactive and engaging.

Name: Nobu Budapest
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Notable sake list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Wheelchair access
Description: Set within a stylish hotel, this chic, minimalist restaurant features well-spaced wooden tables, Japanese lanterns, fretwork screens and an open kitchen. Authentic imported ingredients feature in a huge array of Japanese dishes. For lunch, choose the Bento box; for dinner, the Omakase menu.

Name: Rutin
Description: Set in an affluent city suburb, this chic bistro comes with an appealing buzz and smiles all round. The owner cooks but also keeps a watchful eye over proceedings from his open kitchen near the entrance. Concise menus – supplemented by a few specials – come with creative modern touches and vibrant flavours. Their jazz evenings are very popular.

Name: Bobajka
Address: Andrássy Kúria &  Spa, Fő út 94., Tarcal, 3915, Hungary
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Named after a traditional poppy seed bread pudding from the nearby Zemplén Mountains, Bobajka takes traditional regional dishes like lángos and brassói and gives them a refreshing modern touch. The restaurant is secreted away beneath the Andrássy Kúria & Spa wellness hotel and you can sit either in the vaulted cellar or out on the terrace. Local Tokaj wines are also a draw, with many available by the glass.

Name: White Salon
Description: The New York Palace Hotel provides baroque splendour in spades and its New York Café is the most photographed dining space in Budapest. However, above it, on a mezzanine level, hides this lesser-known jewel, where an enthusiastic team deliver refined, cleanly presented dishes which take inspiration from Hungary’s classics and the former Austro-Hungarian empire. These rich, hearty flavours are balanced by the occasional international note, which adds a welcome freshness to proceedings.

Name: Horgonyzó Kisvendéglő
Description: Simplicity leads the way at this endearing restaurant set just a short stroll from the River Tisza. The room has an unfussy lodge style and there’s plenty of outdoor space courtesy of both a front and rear terrace. Cooking is fresh and well-executed, and offers something for everyone, from Hungarian classics to pizzas, burgers and street food. The wood-fired oven plays a key role, and everything is prepared with love and care.

Name: Clarisse
Address: BOTANIQ Castle, Park utca 37, Tura, 2194, Hungary
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Clarisse is named after the granddaughter of this fairy tale castle’s original owners – and the beautifully furnished dining room is decorated with her art. 10 hectares of forest surround the building and the complex tasting menu reflects this, with courses moving from the soil, via the forest and up to the sky. When it comes to the wine, you can choose either the thoughtfully curated Hungarian pairings or something from the 200-bin cellar. Luxurious bedrooms complete the picture.

Name: Tati
Description: The owners of this restaurant in the up-and-coming District 7 also have a farm on the outskirts of the city where they grow their own fruit and veg. Menus comprise a mix of meat, fish and plant-based creations, with a natural feel to both the appearance and flavour of the dishes. The use of traditional Hungarian recipes results in hearty, wholesome cooking on the dinner menu, while lunch takes on more of a 'brunch' style. The accompanying natural, bio and organic wines come from vineyards in close proximity to the city.

Name: GÓRÉ
Description: A góré is a barn used to dry cereals, and that was this sleek restaurant’s former function – although it's hard to imagine following its chic refurbishment. Climb the stairs to the raised dining area beneath the beams and enjoy the view out through the floor-to-ceiling windows; alternatively, enjoy an al fresco experience on the covered terrace. At the heart of the three tasting menus are strong classical foundations but unique additions offer innovation and originality. The restaurant is quite remotely set, so the comfy bedrooms are a bonus.

Name: MoszkvaTéЯ Bisztró
Address: Monastery Boutique Hotel, Fő utca 30, Budapest, 1011, Hungary
Description: The younger sibling of Arany Kaviár sits on the ground floor of a characterful hotel that was once a monastery. The cuisine here, too, has a Russian theme, with plenty of favourites such as chicken Kiev and some delicious pelmeni (dumplings). The young team are bright and friendly, and a concise list of Hungarian wines completes the picture.

Name: Avalon
Address: H3519 Miskolctapolca, Iglói utca 15, Miskolc, 3519, Hungary
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: Follow the winding road leading up to the Avalon Resort & Spa and look forward to a warm welcome at this sleek restaurant. Pass the tempting array of beautifully crafted desserts into the modern bar with its open kitchen, or head further on into the conservatory. The appealing Italian menu offers everything from pizza and pasta to whole fish and Japanese/Australian Wagyu.

Name: A Konyhám Stúdió 365
Description: Take the lift to the 3rd floor of the Balaton Üzletház shopping mall and you’ll find this bright restaurant with a smart interior and a partial view over the lake. Chef and well-known personality, Gabriella Szikra – kitted out in her trademark cap – has a genuine desire to please, and her modern Hungarian dishes come with bold flavours and arty presentation. Be sure to go for the excellent local wine pairings.

Name: Hoppá! Bistro
Description: This contemporary eatery stands out amongst the myriad choices on vibrant Október Street, both for its smooth service and its modern, well-presented cooking – and it's certainly a popular spot. Large blackboards announce the daily specials, which see traditional Hungarian recipes brought up-to-date, and the excellent value lunch menu is always a hit. Local beers and wines complete the picture.

Name: FLAVA
Description: On the ground floor of the Verno House hotel sits this bustling city hotspot, where elegantly dressed guests fill the room. Grab a seat on the charming street-side terrace and let the slick team guide you through the globally inspired menu where Hungarian, Japanese, Latin American and Middle Eastern influences collide. The contemporary cooking is full of flavour; the steaks and racks of lamb are real draws – as are their smoking cocktails – and be sure to save room for the nougat babka.

Name: LAMAREDA
Description: Lamareda fits into Győr’s beautiful city centre perfectly; think classic Italianate restaurant with service to match. Head past the bistro area at the front to the bright, elegant room behind, where they serve a menu which mixes Hungarian and Mediterranean influences. Good quality ingredients bring flavour to the fore and presentation is detailed; don’t miss the foie gras starter and the zerbó dessert. The daily changing lunch specials are great value and a hit with the locals.

Name: Pajta
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Be sure to arrive early for a wander around the beautiful meadow of this delightfully sympathetic new-build on the edge of the village. The whole place has an elegant, natural feel, and owners Flora and Feri provide the warmest of welcomes and look after their guests so well. The menu changes with the seasons and perfectly reflects the area – for the full experience go at dinner and choose ‘The Path’ menu, with the matching Hungarian wines.

Name: Costes Downtown
Description: Set on the ground floor of the Prestige Hotel, this strikingly decorated restaurant brings nature inside with its living wall and ceiling. Ask for one of the booths or sit at the chef’s table for a view of the kitchen. Set tasting menus offer modern interpretations of Hungarian favourites, with some ambitious flavour combinations and the occasional Asian influence.

Name: Arany Kaviár
Description: French and Russian influences guide the cooking here, which ranges from the simple to the ambitious. Sit in either the opulent, richly appointed dining room or the more modern extension which opens out onto the garden to enjoy the Chef’s Menu – or book the Chef’s Table to sample the World Table Menu. Hungarian and Siberian caviar is a speciality – to start, two caviar tasting menus are offered.

Name: St. Andrea
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: A stylish bar-cum-restaurant with wine-themed décor; owned by a small boutique winery. Well-presented, creative dishes are designed to match their wines – some of which aren’t sold anywhere else in the world! The set lunch menu is a steal.

Name: Mák
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus
Description: From the talented chef to the welcoming service team, everyone immerses themselves in the seasonal ethos at this laid-back restaurant; Chef János Mizsei even takes time out to visit his small, artisan suppliers personally. The tasting menu moves around the country with the seasons – with winter highlighting the north and spring the east, etc. – and János looks to the Nordic kitchen to offer creative versions of classic Hungarian dishes that play with different texture and flavour combinations.

Name: Neked Főztem
Description: This inviting roadside pub sits in an elevated spot and is fronted by a pleasant terrace. Inside it’s warm and welcoming with a rustic feel – thanks to a log burner crackling away on colder nights. Its name translates as ‘I cooked for you’. The concise menu lists all things Hungarian and the friendly team are happy to talk you through it and offer suggestions. The gutsy home-cooking has plenty of flavour and can be paired with a selection of local wines.

Name: Zip's
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus
Description: Don’t be fooled by the rather unassuming exterior, as once inside you are transported to a totally different world... a world of beer! Sit in one of the booths and enjoy a premium beer (some of which are brewed on site), while studying the proudly local, meat-driven menu. The homemade sausages are outstanding, as is the Mangalitsa, and there’s a myriad of different steaks – all of which arrive in generous portions. Service is endearing, and comfortable apartments complete the picture.

Name: Zincenco Kitchen
Description: Offering something a little different, this restaurant is located within a residential apartment, but there’s certainly nothing amateurish or domestic about it; it's even licensed. There are six tables – for a maximum of 14 diners – and all guests are asked to arrive at 7pm, which helps contribute to the supper party atmosphere. You ring doorbell 31 and are greeted by your hosts Zaida Inez Kiss and Igor Zincenco, who go on to fully explain each well-balanced, satisfying dish which features on the modern menu inspired by Hungarian classics.

Name: Alkimista Kulináris Műhely
Description: Its name means ‘Culinary Workshop’ but that feels like doing it an injustice, as this is a beautiful, elegant spot. It's hidden away behind locked gates in a city centre courtyard and everyone is greeted at 7pm by the infectiously enthusiastic chef-owner. Seasonal ingredients feature on a highly personalised tasting menu which cleverly blends the old and the new. Flavours are memorable, sauces are a highlight and the chef describes every dish with heartfelt passion. The price also includes a carefully curated selection of drinks featuring many local biodynamic/organic wines.

Name: Graefl Major Kétútköz
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Wheelchair access
Description: 25 acres of gardens and grounds surround this wonderfully restored art nouveau mansion house – and it is here that they grow, raise and rear all of the produce that is served in the dining room. If it’s in season, you will find it on the menu, from an incredible array of fruit and vegetables to game. They cure their own meats, use their own wheat for the bread, and their beer is an artisan brew. You can also stay overnight in this gloriously peaceful spot.

Name: Öreg Prés
Description: The ‘Old Press’ is a characterful 17C inn which sits in the heart of town; you enter into a pretty courtyard – the perfect spot for a summer’s lunch – and then through into a series of welcoming farmhouse-style rooms. The ambitious chef offers a classic Hungarian menu which is packed with flavour – the well-priced Galloway beef from their own farm is a speciality.

Name: Kreinbacher Birtok
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: At the centre of the Somló Hill vineyard – which specialises in sparkling wines – sits a futuristic collection of buildings, and inside one is a bright brasserie with a contemporary-rustic feel. Influences from Asia and the Mediterranean blend with typical Hungarian flavours, and each dish comes with a suggested pairing from their winery. Comfy bedrooms complete the picture.

Name: Hosszú Tányér
Description: This pretty little restaurant sits in an attractive courtyard setting and is keenly run by its hands-on owners and their friendly team. Inside it’s cool and modern, with fresh flowers on the tables, and open fires feature both inside and out on the terrace. The menu is concise but provides plenty of appeal and the modern Hungarian dishes are full of bold, hearty flavours. A short, all-Hungarian wine list completes the picture.

Name: NOON
Address: Lua Resort, Anna Sétány 3, Balatonfüred, 8230, Hungary
Description: An exclusive lakeside resort plays host to this elegant restaurant (if you’re not staying the night, then pre-booking is essential in high season). Grab a cocktail in the stylish bar before enjoying a carefully curated selection of contemporary Hungarian dishes which fuse tradition with inventive modern touches. Local wines are a feature, and the smooth service shows the team’s knowledge and care. If the chocolate and cherry dessert is on the menu, be sure to choose it.

Name: Rézmozsár
Description: Sitting within part of the old Town Hall, on Kiskunhalas’ pretty main square, this appealing bistro presents traditional Hungarian dishes in their best light. Cooking is satisfying and full of flavour, and care and attention is put into the presentation. The menu changes daily, although the house specials are not to be missed – especially the apple pie crêpes. Wood, brick and booths help to create a cosy, rustic feel.

Name: Botanica
Address: Hotel Botanica, Nyárfa utca 47, Dánszentmiklós, 2735, Hungary
Description: Lovely gardens surround this delightful, family-owned country house, which comes with bespoke designer bedrooms and charming service. Start with a drink in one of the comfortable lounges before heading through to the elegant restaurant, where a spot on the terrace is a must in summer. The 4 course menu offers two choices at each course; traditional Hungarian flavours are to the fore in refined, modern creations.

Name: Lokal47
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: At Kristinus Wine Estate's HQ, not only do they bottle and sell their wines, but you have the chance to try them alongside some delicious dishes either inside their restaurant or out on the large terrace. Its name derives from their farm 47kms away, and they supplement this source of produce with as many local suppliers as possible. The frequently changing menu comprises tasty small plates that go perfectly with their wines. There are also modern bedrooms available on the estate.

Name: Tihanyi Vinarius
Description: Take in lovely views over the countryside and the lake from the terrace of this charming thatched building dating from 1822. The interior is full of historic character – it even boasts a hidden vaulted brick-built room which is used for private events – and the formal service suits the style of the place. Some unusual and rarely seen ingredients feature in well-crafted dishes; Tihany is famous for its lavender, so the ‘vinarius 200 tortaszelet’ dessert is a must.

Name: Hey Kiddo
Description: High above Tennyson Street, Hey Kiddo is one of Denver's trendiest restaurants. From the third floor location to the eclectic menu, there is nothing typical about this hot spot. Chef Kelly Whitaker mans the stoves, taking full liberties with an ever-changing menu. There's something for everyone, with oysters, caviar, K-town fried chicken, shrimp toast, crudo and pasta dishes among the tempting options. Flavors and inspiration come from around the world, as in shaken beef that's as much fun as it is delicious. Tonnarelli tossed with asparagus, mushrooms and parmesan is hit with an Asian sauce for a winning dish, and the quirkiness continues through dessert, where rice cream with burnt banana can be topped with sancho, broken cone, lingonberry or caramel.

Name: Guard and Grace
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Guard and Grace occupies an enviable location at the base of the 56-floor Brookfield Building in downtown Denver. Expectations at this restaurant in one of the city's tallest skyscrapers are deservedly high, as this ultra-sleek space delivers day and night. The vast space is stunning, with an oak fire roaring in the open kitchen, a floor-to ceiling wine room and a sophisticated blend of modernity and rusticity. Steaks are the obvious draw but a full seafood bar is a close second. Artichoke and spinach dip is a rich and flavorful starter before tucking in to filet mignon with lime smashed potatoes and chili butter. Chocolate Luxardo cherry cheesecake sided by a scoop of honey Bourbon ice cream is nothing short of indulgent.

Name: A5 Steakhouse
Description: With its prime corner location, large picture windows and beautifully framed doors, A5 Steakhouse beckons diners with an instant warmth. Inside, an attractive bar is particularly welcoming, especially at happy hour, while the dining room shares a retro vibe complete with kitschy artwork. The kitchen is headed by Partner/Chef Max MacKissock who doles out classic steakhouse favorites with slight variations, as in a wedge salad with cubes of avocado, tomato confit, pickled red onion and crisp guanciale doused in Roquefort dressing. The Denver steak does its namesake proud, with anterior chuck from Blackhawk Farms, KY, flawless technique and taste that warrant a return visit. To finish, choose the banana creme brûlée with spiced sour cherry preserves.

Name: Stella's Cucina
Description: The entrance flies a bit under the radar (hint: look for the "S" on the door), but once inside owner Stella Spanu's Italian gem, nothing is held back. The place is utterly stunning with a discernible 1930s sexy speakeasy ambience. Chef Filippo Piccini impresses with a focused menu of pan-regional Italian dishes. If comfort is what you need, start with ribollita, that traditional, thick Tuscan soup brimming with vegetables, beans and silky bread. Limone e uova di mare offers a dramatic presentation with a nest of spaghettone alla chitarra, while Milanese di vitello, with a properly thick chop of satiny Limousin veal, is a special for good reason. Finally, babà al rum is an elegant ode to one of Naples' best-known desserts.

Name: Prospect
Description: Located in the swanky, studiously hip Hotel Jerome, it’s not hard to see why Prospect is one of the hottest restaurants in Aspen. The colorful, eclectic space mirrors the au courant menu, as in kimchi rösti with a fried egg and okonomiyaki sauce, or chèvre ravioli with Calabrian chili, charred broccolini, and golden fig. Eye-catching desserts, like an intricate, architectural composition of mocha savarin, dark chocolate and passion fruit caramel, offer a fitting finale. Not that any further enticements are necessary, but a compelling cocktail program provides tipples for every taste (including non-alcoholic options)—just one more reason for the influencer set to snap photos.

Name: WYLD
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Brunch,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Nestled inside The Ritz-Carlton, Bachelor Gulch, this sophisticated restaurant is far from wild. Instead, it's the very picture of rustic refinement right down to the large windows framing postcard-perfect views of Beaver Creek. Settle in to this laid-back luxe spot and share stories of the day's alpine adventures over likeable dishes like salsa macha atop a crisp tostada with avocado aioli and slices of albacore. Earthy red and yellow beets rest over a creamy, tart tzatziki sprinkled with toasted pumpernickel breadcrumbs in a refreshing first course. Heartier entrees, like chicken under a brick with roasted carrots, parsnips and celery root puree, are especially satisfying after epic days filled with skiing or hiking.

Name: Boulder Dushanbe Tea House
Description: This hand-built gift from Dushanbe, Boulder's sister city in Tajikistan, offers a respite from quotidian life. Walk through the front garden and you'll be instantly transported to a zen-filled, magical space. If the bucolic setting doesn't lower your blood pressure, the stunning interior that transports you to a faraway culture will. As the name suggests, tea is the raison d'être here, and the selection is comprehensive. From apple strudel and samosas to feijoada and plov (a buttery rice dish studded with chickpeas, dried fruit and grilled beef), the menu reads like a world explorer's diary. Naturally, tea time and afternoon tea are reason alone to visit, and the dessert selection is particularly tempting.

Name: Noisette
Description: Chefs Tim Lu and Lillian Cho earned their chops in some of New York's top restaurants but thankfully chose Denver to open their own place. Sophisticated and spacious with a separate patisserie up front, the dining room is elegant, but the real draw is the precisely crafted dishes bound by tradition while reflecting a creative approach. Foie gras au torchon with a light coating of Björn's lavender honey and a Port reduction is served with a buttery brioche for a classic take.
